n-from-four-features-to-the-population.title: From four features to the whole dictionary
n-from-four-features-to-the-population.intro: The parent gave the results of the population analysis. This level gives the machinery that produced them: which units were dropped before scoring, what the rater and the language model were actually shown, what happens to the numbers when the sampling bias is corrected properly, and how much of the layer the reconstruction stands in for.

chapters.title: Who gets scored, and against what
chapters.body:
Before a single unit is rated, the population is trimmed. The A/1 dictionary has 4,096 learned features. 168 of them are [[dead-neurons|dead]]: active on none of the 100 million dataset examples checked. Another 292 are [[ultralow-density-cluster|ultralow density]], firing on fewer than about one token in a million and showing other atypical properties.

Both groups are excluded from the analysis. So the population claim covers roughly 3,636 features, about 89% of the dictionary. The cut is made on firing rate rather than on how the units would have scored, but it is still a cut, and [[global-analysis-framing|the paper's framing of this section]] is explicit that several nearby questions remain unanswered.

The rater is one of the authors, Adam Jermyn, [[blinded-annotation|working blind]] — shown a unit without being told whether it came from the autoencoder or from the MLP's own neurons.

The rubric [[rubric-interpretation-first|asks for an interpretation first]] and scores the evidence against it afterwards. Then [[feature-interpretability-rubric|five numbers]]. Confidence in the interpretation, 0–3. Consistency of the high-activation tokens with it, 0–5. Consistency of the positive logit effects, 0–3. [[rubric-effect-size-separation|One further point]] if the inconsistent logit effects were at least clearly smaller than the consistent ones. Specificity, 0–3.

Those add to 15, but the ceiling is 14. A perfect 3 on logit consistency leaves the separation item with nothing to be about.

The sampling is what costs. Each unit's range is cut into eleven evenly spaced [[activation-interval|bands]], and examples are drawn from each, because reading only [[top-dataset-examples|the strongest firings]] is [[max-dataset-example-bias|exactly what makes a mixed unit look clean]].

Scoring a band by hand is slow. 412 bands were scored across 162 units. Eleven bands apiece would have been 1,782, so under a quarter of the available bands were ever looked at. [[fig-39|The resulting histograms]] are built on that.

sections.title: How Interpretable is the Typical Feature?

chapters.title: What the automated rater is actually shown
chapters.body:
The explanation step gives Claude 2 [[explanation-generation-setup|forty-nine examples of a unit]], composed deliberately: ten from the top band, two from each of the remaining bands, five completely random, and ten where the unit's top-activating token appears in other contexts. That last group is there to separate a token detector from a token-in-context detector. The model also gets the unit's top and bottom logits, labels saying which band each example came from, and eight worked demonstrations on held-out units showing chain-of-thought reasoning.

Activations are [[activation-quantization|rounded to integers 0 through 9]] throughout. The model is asked to be succinct and not to name the specific tokens it fires on.

The prediction step happens in a fresh interaction with [[no-activation-leakage|no true activations visible]]. Sixty examples: six from the top band, two from each other band, ten completely random, twenty top-activating tokens out of context. They are shuffled, the logits and band labels are stripped, and blanks are left for the model to fill.

All sixty are scored in one pass for cost; the paper says each ideally would be its own prompt. Nine tokens each gives [[activation-prediction-scoring|540 predictions]], and the score is [[spearman-correlation|their rank correlation]] with the truth.

That sampling is where it departs from the prior work it follows, which scored on maximal examples mixed with random text. For a feature firing once in $10^5$ tokens, that mostly tests whether the model can tell a large activation from zero.

When Claude predicts one constant value — usually all zeros — [[constant-prediction-zero-score|no correlation exists and the unit is given 0]], which is the spike at the left of [[fig-40|the score histogram]]. [[pearson-correlation|Linear correlation]] gives [[fig-69|nearly the same picture]].

[[automated-logit-scoring|The logit variant]] shows 100 tokens per unit: 50 random, and 50 drawn from the 10th to 60th largest positive [[logit-weight|logit weights]], since the top ten went into the explanation. [[fig-41|Features answer better]].

chapters.title: Where the evidence is thinnest
chapters.body:
[[activation-interval-analysis|Scoring bands separately]] asks a different question from scoring a unit: does this range of activations fit the hypothesis the whole unit suggested? [[fig-42|The answer splits two ways]]. Many features are consistent across their entire range. Others hold across roughly the top 60% and then fall away quickly.

The paper offers [[feature-at-slight-angle|one possible cause]] and does not test it. If a learned direction sits slightly off the direction it was meant to find, strong firings still come from the intended cause, while weak ones pick up whatever else has a small projection onto it.

That matters because of the first of [[interpretability-evaluation-caveats|two caveats the paper states]]. [[low-interval-activation-skew|Most real activations are small]], so most of the firing mass lands in the bands that score worst. The paper's counter is that [[large-activations-dominate|the effect on the output is carried by the strong firings]], which are the interpretable ones.

[[interpretability-importance-caveat|The second caveat]] is that units were sampled uniformly, and interpretability might track importance. The authors say their impression is that the most active features are more interpretable, not less. They did not run that experiment.

There is a third problem the main text does not present as a caveat. [[importance-scoring|Reweighting the automated score]] to what genuinely random text would have given is the principled correction: random examples get weight 1, band examples get [[feature-density|feature density]] times the band's probability.

[[importance-scoring-degeneracy|The correction eats itself]]. With densities around $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$, nearly all weight lands on random text where the feature never fires. Predicting zero everywhere then scores well, and any false positive rate is punished hard.

[[fig-71|Under that weighting]] features still beat neurons, 0.28 against 0.04, but both collapse toward zero. The headline figures are the unweighted ones.

chapters.title: Splicing the dictionary back into the model
chapters.body:
The substitution is mechanical. Run the transformer normally as far as the MLP, take the activation vector, throw it away, put the autoencoder's reconstruction of it in its place, and finish the forward pass. The log-likelihood loss goes up by some amount.

That amount alone means nothing without a scale. [[zero-ablation-baseline|The scale chosen]] is the loss increase from deleting the MLP layer altogether — the whole of what the layer contributes. Divide one by the other. The substitution penalty is 21% of the deletion penalty, so [[loss-recovered-by-features|79% of the layer's loss contribution is recovered]].

Note what this is not. It measures how well the reconstruction stands in, not whether the features are readable; a good reconstruction made of uninterpretable directions would score the same.

It is also a dial rather than a property of the method. Widen the dictionary or lower [[l1-coefficient|the sparsity penalty]] and the number rises. [[dictionary-learning-run|Run]] A/5, with 131,072 features and a coefficient of 0.004, recovers 94.5% — bought with far more active features per token, which is [[l0-nll-tradeoff|the tradeoff]] [[fig-68|the sweep plots directly]].

[[loss-recovery-caveats|The paper distrusts its own number]] on two grounds. Fraction of loss may be the wrong frame, since it expects a long tail where each further percent costs many more features. And the features are not fully [[monosemanticity|monosemantic]], with some mixing possibly hiding in low activations, so what is being counted is not a clean set of [[true-features|true features]].

The measure it would rather have is [[explanation-based-loss-measure|substitution from explanations]]: replace activations with what the written interpretations predict. Naively that needs one sample of the explaining model per feature per token. The paper puts 100k features on one 4,096-token context at $12,500–$25,000, and you would need many contexts.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: Whether any of this is about the model
chapters.body:
The autoencoder is fit to MLP activations and nothing else. Those activations are [[pile-dataset|the Pile]] pushed through embedding, attention and the MLP, so structure in the dictionary could come from the corpus rather than from anything the transformer learned. [[model-vs-data-question|That is the objection]].

The control is built by [[weight-shuffling|shuffling the entries within each weight matrix]] of the trained Run A model. Shuffling rather than resampling keeps the distribution of individual weights exactly as it was, so whatever the shuffle destroys is structure and only structure. [[randomized-transformer|Dictionary learning is then run on that model]].

What comes out is many single-token features — "span", "file", ".", "nature" — and features firing on arbitrary-looking subsets of recognizable contexts such as LaTeX or code. The authors report that they could not build interpretations of the non-single-token ones that made much sense, and invite readers to check the visualization themselves.

On the automated activation score, [[fig-70|the shuffled model's features score slightly higher]] than the real ones. The paper does not soften this.

Its response is to split the population. [[single-token-features|A feature counts as single-token]] when the same token carries the largest activation in all twenty top-band examples. The shuffled model's are both more numerous and more purely single-token, firing on that token even in the weakest bands, which makes them close to free to predict. [[randomized-feature-bimodality|Once the two clusters are separated]], the real features win on the rest, and the shuffled remainder looks like the polysemantic neurons.

The structural argument is separate and stronger. [[downstream-effects-outside-dictionary-learning|The MLP output weights and unembedding are never inputs to the autoencoder]], so agreement between what a feature fires on and what it writes cannot be an artifact of the fit. Logit inspection, [[feature-ablation|ablation]] and [[pinned-feature-sampling|pinning]] all test that, and [[fig-43|pinned sampling]] is the one the shuffled control cannot imitate.

n-the-same-features-twice.title: The same features in a second model
n-the-same-features-twice.intro: The parent gave the results. This level is about the instruments: what each of the three similarity measures actually computes over what index set, why two of them disagree by construction rather than by accident, and how much weight the comparison against neurons can carry.

chapters.title: Describing a feature without naming a model
chapters.body:
A feature in [[dictionary-learning-run|run]] A/1 is a direction in one transformer's 512-dimensional MLP activation space. A feature in B/1 is a direction in a different 512-dimensional space. The two spaces have the same dimension and nothing else in common, because [[transformer-a-and-b|the second transformer]] built its hidden basis from its own initialization.

So the vectors cannot be compared directly. Cosine similarity between dictionary columns — what [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]] measures between two dictionaries fit to the same activations — has nothing to hold onto here.

[[universality|The question]] has to be asked about something outside both models.

The paper's [[activation-similarity|first description]] is a feature's behaviour on data. Fix a corpus, position by position: 40,960,000 tokens of [[pile-dataset|the Pile]]. Every feature in either model becomes a vector of that length, holding its activation at each position. Two features are similar when those vectors correlate.

The shape of those vectors matters. Feature activations are non-negative, and most features fire on far fewer than one token in a thousand — [[feature-density|density]] is the paper's term. Nearly every entry is therefore zero in both vectors.

A Pearson correlation over such a pair is decided almost entirely by the handful of positions where at least one of the two fires.

The search itself is one-directional. For each of the 4,096 features in A/1, the paper takes the argmax over all 4,096 features in B/1. Nothing prevents two A features from claiming the same B partner.

That is exactly what you would expect if the two dictionaries carved the same territory at slightly different grain, which is what [[feature-splitting]] describes. The paper reads the low-correlation tail the same way: those pairs may be splittings that fell differently, or genuinely different things the two base models learned. [[feature-notation|The A/1 and B/1 labels]] carry that structure — model, then run, then feature index.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

chapters.title: Why the second measure reads low
chapters.body:
The second description is what a feature does rather than when it fires. Firing adds the feature's direction to the MLP output, and that addition travels through the unembedding to every next-token logit. In this model the path is [[linear-logit-effects|close to linear in the activation]], so it collapses to one number per vocabulary entry. That vector is the [[logit-weight]], and [[logit-weight-similarity|correlating two of them]] is the second measure.

The trouble is the vector's shape. [[logit-weight-histogram|Its histogram]] is bimodal: a tall mode sitting at zero that covers nearly the whole vocabulary, plus a small mode far to the right holding the tokens the feature is about. The paper reads the tall mode as [[weight-interference|weight interference]] — weights the model would prefer at zero but cannot have, because the feature shares its space with others.

A Pearson correlation over tens of thousands of vocabulary entries gives every entry equal say. Almost all of them sit in the interference mode. If that mode is noise, the number is largely a correlation between two independent noises. (The plots do drop [[anomalous-token-exclusion|never-used vocabulary elements]], but that trims a tail, not the mode.)

[[fig-19|The Arabic pair's scatter]] shows the same bimodality in two dimensions: Arabic tokens cluster together at the top right, and the centre is a round, uncorrelated cloud.

[[fig-53|The population version]] places every matched pair at its two correlations, and the mass sits below the diagonal.

[[logit-weight-disagreement|The 0.98-and-negative pair]] is the same effect with the sign flipped. Zoom the inset and only the period is high in both models. Every other token is interference.

The paper's suggestion is that the model may simply not care what a feature does to tokens already made implausible by [[direct-path|the direct path]], by attention, or by other MLP features. It says "may".

One aside falls out of the same pair. The feature fires on 0.02% of tokens, so at least one Pile token in ten thousand is a PLoS abbreviation inside a citation.

chapters.title: Weighting by what the model actually needed
chapters.body:
The instrument the paper says it wants ignores the vocabulary and asks about effects on data. Ablate a feature: [[eq-feature-ablation|subtract its activation times its dictionary direction]] from the MLP output, then run the rest of the model and record how much worse the prediction gets at that position.

Do that for every feature at every position and each feature becomes a vector of ablation effects indexed by datapoint. Two features whose ablations hurt the same predictions must have been supplying the same thing — which is [[feature-downstream-effects|the notion of effect]] the paper uses elsewhere.

It does not do this. Count the cost: a separate forward pass for each of 4,096 features at each sampled position.

[[attribution-similarity|The substitute]] keeps the index set and drops the forward passes. At position $t_j$, take the feature's activation $f_i(t_j)$. Look up its [[logit-weight]] $v_{it_{j+1}}$ on the token that actually came next. [[eq-attribution-vector|Multiply the two]]:

$$f_i(t_j)\,v_{i t_{j+1}}$$

Stack that over a random sample of datapoints and you have the [[attribution-vector]].

The product does two things at once. It zeroes out every position where the feature was silent. And where the feature did fire, it selects from the whole logit-weight vector the single entry the data made relevant.

The paper notes this is the standard gradient-times-activation attribution, minus the softmax denominator and minus the layer norm denominator — [[layer-norm-linearization|the same linearization]] it uses to get logit weights at all.

[[fig-54|Attribution correlation plotted against activation correlation]] lands close to the diagonal, and the paper treats that as licence to use activation correlation throughout.

It is worth being exact about what that shows. The attribution vector is indexed by datapoint and is zero wherever the activation is zero, so it shares its support with the activation vector by construction. Some of the agreement is guaranteed before any fact about the model enters. The paper does not separate that part out, and it belongs alongside [[logit-weight-caveats|its other stated caveats]] about reading logit weights.

chapters.title: The control: the same test run on neurons
chapters.body:
Nothing so far says whether 0.72 is a large number. A median correlation has no natural scale to be read against.

So the paper runs the identical procedure on the units the architecture already supplied. Same two transformers, same 40 million positions, same argmax search — but over [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|the 512 MLP neurons]] instead of the dictionary. It is the cross-model version of [[most-correlated-neuron|the nearest-neuron search]] used on individual features. [[fig-52|The two histograms]] are drawn together.

Median 0.72 for features. Median 0.46 for neurons.

The neuron number is the more interesting half. It is well above zero, so two independently seeded transformers do produce partly matching neurons.

That is what [[polysemanticity]] predicts. If a neuron is a mixture of several features, and both models learn roughly the same features, their mixtures overlap even when the mixing itself is arbitrary. The [[privileged-basis|neuron basis]] is singled out by the elementwise nonlinearity, not by holding one thing per coordinate — which is the point [[feature-neuron-nonalignment|the per-feature checks]] made one feature at a time.

[[feature-vs-neuron-universality|The gap between the two medians]] is the claim.

One thing the comparison does not control. Each A feature is matched against 4,096 candidates; each A neuron against 512. A maximum over eight times as many candidates runs higher in expectation, even for unrelated units. No matched-pool version is reported, so the sign of the gap is easier to trust than its size.

And the scope stays narrow. Two seeds, one architecture, one dataset. [[feature-universality|The per-feature universality checks]] earlier in the paper — Arabic at 0.91, DNA at 0.92, Hebrew at 0.92, base64 at 0.85 — all point at this same model B.

chapters.title: Matching against other people's models
chapters.body:
Everything above compares two models built to be comparable: same architecture, same data, same hyperparameters, corpus positions that line up index for index. [[universality-with-the-literature|The stronger question]] is whether features recur across models sharing none of that.

Here the method itself breaks. Activation correlation needs both units evaluated at the same positions, and a neuron reported in someone else's model on someone else's data cannot be put on that axis. What is left is the authors reading published descriptions and judging resemblance.

The closest comparison is to one-layer models trained with [[solu|the SoLU activation]], an earlier attempt to make neurons monosemantic through architecture rather than through decomposition afterwards. Three of its interpretable neurons — base64, hexadecimal, all caps — reappear here as features in [[dictionary-resolution|the smallest dictionary]]: A/0/45, A/0/119, A/0/317.

[[solu-base64-neuron|The base64 case]] came first and is the one the paper leans on. [[base64-feature|The base64 feature]] turned up so reliably that its presence became a debugging check on new [[dictionary-learning]] runs, alongside [[hexadecimal-feature|its hexadecimal neighbour]]. Universality was a workflow tool before it was a result.

Three further comparisons are offered. Dictionary learning applied to the residual stream reports a German detector and title-case detectors, matched here by A/0/493 and A/0/508, and also reports the same abundance of [[single-token-features|single-token features]]. [[sparse-probing|Sparse probing]] work yields a prime-factors feature, A/4/22414, and a French feature, A/0/14. [[multimodal-neurons|Multimodal neurons]] in vision-language models include region neurons, loosely mirrored by Australia, Canada, Africa and Israel-Palestine features in run A/3.

The paper reports where the parallel fails. Its person detectors are narrow — A/1/3240 responds to one name in one kind of context, called only "somewhat similar" to a Trump neuron. Nothing found here resembles an emotion neuron.

The section's verb is "we believe". No number is attached to any of it.

n-what-the-collection-looks-like.title: What the Whole Collection Looks Like
n-what-the-collection-looks-like.intro: The level above named the kinds of feature and the reframings that follow from them. This one supplies the numbers behind those names, the constructions that produced the geometry, and the several places where the paper's evidence is thinner than the claim it supports.

chapters.title: The catalogue, and the number that surprised them
chapters.body:
[[phenomenology]] is the paper's own word for this stretch of work, borrowed from physics. It means taking a theory you already accept and using it to reason about what a system does.

The authors are careful about how much they will claim from it. They say the features vary so much that no concise summary captures them, and they point readers at the browsing interface rather than write an inventory. What follows is a set of abstract patterns instead.

The [[feature-motifs]] they name come with a structural rationale attached, offered as a guess rather than a result. An attention head largely computes what the paper calls a three-point function: two inputs, one output. An MLP layer is better placed to compute a conjunction over many tokens at once.

[[context-features]] and [[token-in-context-features]] are the far end of that — a conjunction spanning a whole passage — so the authors say it is perhaps natural that these dominate.

The sheer volume is what struck them. In run A/4, one of the large dictionaries, more than a hundred features respond primarily to the token "the".

A word on that naming. A [[dictionary-learning-run]] is one trained autoencoder, labelled A/0 through A/4. A/0 learns 512 features, matching the transformer's MLP width exactly; A/1 learns 4,096; A/2 learns 16,384.

[[trigram-features]] sit at the small end of the range. Feature A/2/12310 predicts "19" after "COVID-". Attention alone could implement that continuation in principle, and the paper notes the model recruits the MLP layer for it anyway.

[[memorization-features]] sit at the other extreme, and surface only in the largest runs.

chapters.title: Every feature is also a move
chapters.body:
Why is the action reading available at all? In a one-layer transformer the MLP is the last one, so its output reaches the logits along a single linear path: the MLP output weights, then the unembedding. That makes a feature's [[logit-weight]] vector — one number per vocabulary token — readable directly as what the feature pushes for. Read that way, every feature is both a detector and an [[action-features|action]].

The reading earns its keep on an anomaly. Feature A/0/341 was labelled "the" in mathematical prose. Its top positive logits are generic mathematical nouns: denominator, remainder, theorem.

It also fires on "special" and "this", which are not "the". Read as an action — predict a noun phrase in mathematical text — those firings stop being impurities, since adjectives are followed by noun phrases too.

Chaining follows from there. The simplest case is a [[self-exciting-feature-loop]]: the [[base64-feature]] raises the probability of tokens like Qg and zA, which are exactly the tokens that make it fire again ([[fig-55]]). Two nodes next — one feature on all-caps word pieces, one on underscores, alternating to build ARRAY_MAX_VALUE ([[fig-56]]). [[unicode-token-state-machines|Split Unicode characters]] give the same shape, since ண arrives as a block byte followed by a character byte.

The paper's caution about [[finite-state-automata-features|these assemblies]] is specific. The [[html-feature-automaton|four-node HTML system]] of [[fig-58]] is simple only because A/0 is small; A/1 would be far messier. It is also already incomplete — nothing in it covers what happens when the tag-name feature emits href.

[[fig-59]] shows an entirely separate system for IRC transcripts. [[fig-60]] shows three narrow A/4 features reciting license boilerplate, which the paper reads as memorization and as a case of [[mechanistic-anomaly-detection]], while noting that mechanisms buried this deep in superposition are likely noisy.

chapters.title: Widening the dictionary, one feature at a time
chapters.body:
Walk the base64 case, because the paper does.

In A/0 there is one [[base64-feature]], A/0/45, and it fires on every token of a base64 string. In A/1 three features jointly cover the same ground ([[fig-48]]). A/1/2357 leans on letters, A/1/2364 leans on digits, and those two predict largely the same tokens with one difference: the digit feature has much lower logit weights on digits ([[fig-49]]).

That difference is not semantic. It is the tokenizer. A single digit followed by another digit would have been merged — [Bq][8][9][mp] never occurs, because 89 tokenizes as one token. So a current token that is a lone digit genuinely does say the next token is not a digit, even in random base64.

The third feature, A/1/1544, had no obvious rule. The clue was the token ICAgICAg, which decodes to six spaces. It fires on base64 that decodes to readable ASCII ([[fig-50]]).

[[feature-splitting]] also cleaned up an apparent bug pointing the other way. Coarse runs produce high-magnitude features that fire on every instance of the token " P" — pointless, since bigram statistics could do that without spending MLP capacity. In wider dictionaries that single feature resolves into sixteen or more P features in different contexts ([[fig-47]]). The base64 trio is the converse case, [[multiple-features-for-one-context|several features for what looks like one context]].

To link features across runs the paper defines [[masked-cosine-similarity]]. Restrict to the tokens where the first feature fires and correlate the two activation vectors there; repeat on the tokens where the second fires; keep the larger number. Draw an edge above roughly 0.4 — a threshold chosen to keep the graph readable, not for any principled reason, with ultralow-density features dropped.

The resulting graph ([[fig-46]]) is not a tree: [[splitting-is-not-a-tree|features both split and merge]] between sizes. And the finer features predict differently, not merely activate differently — A/2/2609 supports the gauge, the Lagrangian, the spacetime.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: Where the directions actually sit
chapters.body:
The geometry claim rests on a specific construction, and it is worth knowing what was fed in. Each feature is represented by its column of the decoder matrix — a 512-vector, one entry per MLP neuron. Those vectors from three runs are embedded by [[umap|UMAP]] into two dimensions with a cosine metric, 15 neighbours, and a minimum distance of 0.01.

The coloured clusters do not come from that plot. They come from [[hdbscan-feature-clustering|HDBSCAN]] run on a separate 10-dimensional UMAP of the same vectors.

So [[feature-umap|the projection]] is a display of neighbourhoods, not of distances. Reading [[fig-44]] as a map with meaningful gaps would be reading more than the method supports.

What it does support is [[feature-geometry-clusters|small angles within a family]]. The base64 features sit near each other; the Arabic ones sit near each other.

From this the paper conjectures [[true-features]]: an idealized set that [[dictionary-learning]] would return at unlimited size, often already clustered tightly in the model. A finite dictionary returns directions covering approximately the same territory, at the cost of specificity ([[fig-45]]). Different sizes are then [[dictionary-resolution|resolutions of one object]] — and the authors go further, saying that under some versions of their theory the [[correct-number-of-features]] may not be well posed at all.

The revision to [[isotropic-superposition-model|the inherited picture]], where features are discrete, one-dimensional and pushed apart by interference into a roughly even spread, has two candidate causes. Features might clump because they fire together. Or — the paper suspects this matters more — because they act alike: the digit and letter base64 features predict nearly the same tokens, and similar output actions land as similar directions.

[[theories-of-superposition|The revised account]] adds [[feature-manifolds]] as a separate possibility ([[fig-61]]). The paper is careful that this is two hypotheses rather than one, and that some manifolds would admit no finite description in one-dimensional features.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: One unit per combination, and why that is suspicious
chapters.body:
Some [[token-in-context-features|token-in-context features]] are unobjectionable. "die" in German is the definite article; "die" in English is a death or a dice. Representing those separately is what you would want.

"the" in Physics as against "the" in mathematics is not like that. The paper says plainly that these were not what it expected to find in a one-layer model.

[[local-vs-compositional-codes|The framing]] makes the question askable. A [[compositional-code]] has a unit for "the" and a unit for Physics, and lets both be active. A [[local-code]] has a unit for the pair. The observed features are a local code, and the two hypotheses are that the transformer uses one, or that [[dictionary-learning]] imposed one.

The second is a real worry, because of the objective. The loss adds $\lambda \sum_i |f_i|$ to the reconstruction error, so [[l1-sparsity-penalty|the sparsity term]] charges per active unit, scaled by [[l1-coefficient|the coefficient]]. A local code fires one unit where a compositional code fires two. The penalty therefore prefers the local answer whatever the transformer is doing, which means the method may be producing exactly what it appears to find.

[[are-token-in-context-features-real|The paper's reply]] is not an experiment. It is [[sharper-predictions-argument|an argument about what each scheme can express]].

Under a compositional code, the logits in physics text after "the" are forced to be a sum of two generic vectors: what usually follows "the", plus what is common in physics. Nothing sharper than that sum is reachable. A local code can attach any logit vector it likes to the combination, and the model may want that.

The hedging is the paper's own. It says only that it believes the second hypothesis holds to some extent, and grants that better dictionary learning schemes might yet recover a more compositional set from the same transformer.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not.title: Which run to keep, and what the paper settled
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not.intro: The level above named four signals and a list of limits. This one says what each signal is actually computed from, what number gets read off it, where it stops working — and then walks the paper's own accounting of what its result is and is not worth.

chapters.title: Why there is no test loss here
chapters.body:
In ordinary machine learning you would settle this with a held-out loss. The autoencoder does have a loss, and it is trained on it: squared reconstruction error plus a sparsity term. So the first thing to explain is why that number cannot do the job.

The obstacle is that the loss function is not the same function across the runs being compared. [[l1-coefficient|A scalar $\lambda$]] sets the exchange rate between [[mse-reconstruction-term|the reconstruction term]] and the sparsity penalty. Change $\lambda$ and you have changed the objective itself, so two resulting numbers are not measurements of the same quantity.

[[training-loss-metric|Training loss]] therefore stays useful only inside a fixed $\lambda$. The paper uses it to compare optimizers, learning rates and training lengths, and for nothing else.

Even a comparable loss would be aimed at the wrong target. What the paper wants is a dictionary whose entries a person can read, and nothing in the objective mentions that.

So the authors went looking for a criterion that did. The proposal was to score a factorization by the total information of the autoencoder plus the data, preferring whichever factorization describes the data most cheaply. [[information-based-metric|It did not work]], and the way it failed is specific.

Total information did not track subjective interpretability. It did not track sparsity either. A run in which hundreds of features fired on the average token, but which reconstructed the activations closely, could come out with lower total information than a run with far fewer active features and worse reconstruction.

The criterion scored well exactly the solutions the paper wanted to reject.

What is left is a bundle. [[toy-model-ground-truth|Synthetic setups whose true features are known by construction]] gave a clean check early on, [[feature-exploration-interface|a published browser]] makes [[manual-inspection|looking at features]] cheap enough to do often, and the authors say outright that they have [[recognizing-good-features|no systematic way to tell a good run from a bad one]]. [[evaluating-dictionary-learning|The evaluation]] is that admission written out.

chapters.title: Two numbers, and the curve between them
chapters.body:
Two of the four signals are numbers you can put on a pair of axes, and the paper does exactly that.

The first is [[l0-norm|the $L^0$ norm]] of the sparse code: the average count of nonzero feature activations on a token. It is not a loss, and nothing is optimized against it directly. It only says how many pieces the decomposition actually uses.

The paper has no principled target for it. The working rule is to aim below 10 or 20, and to distrust any solution where $L^0$ is a large fraction of the layer's width. For [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|the model under study]] that width is 512, and a code with a hundred-odd active entries is not buying much over reading the neurons directly.

The second number substitutes the autoencoder into the model. Run the MLP activations through it, put the reconstruction back in place of the real activations, and measure the loss on the training data. The raw increase is hard to read on its own.

So it is divided by [[zero-ablation-baseline|the increase you get from deleting the MLP layer altogether]]. For A/1 the substitution costs 21% of what deletion costs, which is where [[loss-recovered-by-features|79% recovered]] comes from.

[[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat|The paper distrusts its own denominator]]. A transformer with its MLP zeroed may be an especially bad thing to measure against. Ad hoc experiments the paper does not show reached similarly high percentages by training a transformer from scratch with a small MLP.

[[l0-nll-tradeoff|Put the two numbers on axes]] and every trained run lands somewhere. In [[fig-68]] each line is one value of $\lambda$, and the points along a line are dictionary widths running from 512 up to 131,072. [[sparsity-versus-explained-loss-sweep|The lines all slope the same way]]: a weaker penalty lets more features fire and recovers more of the loss.

A/5 sits at the loose end, with 131,072 features, $\lambda = 0.004$ and 94.5% recovered. A/1 sits at the sparse end with 79%.

Nothing on the plot says which end is right.

chapters.title: The histogram you check first
chapters.body:
The third signal is the one the authors reach for most while iterating, because it costs almost nothing to compute.

[[feature-density|A feature's density]] is the fraction of tokens on which it takes a nonzero value. Every feature in these dictionaries is rare. The interesting question is how rare, and how the rarities are spread across a run — so the densities go into a histogram on a log axis.

[[feature-density-diagnostics|Three numbers get read off it]]. How many live features sit outside the ultralow mode. The lowest density at which features outside that mode still appear, which says how rare a feature the run managed to find at all. And how many features fire on more than 1% of tokens, where a large count is taken as a sign that $\lambda$ is too low.

Ideally a hidden unit would be either a real feature or [[dead-neurons|completely dead]], and dead ones are [[neuron-resampling|periodically reinitialized]] during training. What shows up instead is a third category.

[[fig-64]] is the standard picture, for run A/16. There is [[ultralow-density-cluster|a spike around one token in ten million]] and [[high-density-cluster|a broad mode around one in a hundred thousand]]. The paper adds that the right mode may itself be two modes, and says it is still investigating that.

Then the diagnostic stops working. In [[fig-65]], a run with 131,072 hidden units and a large $\lambda$, the two modes overlap and cannot be read apart.

[[density-cluster-separation|The repair is to add two more coordinates]]: each feature's encoder bias, and the dot product between its encoder and decoder vectors. In those three dimensions the high-density cluster separates cleanly again ([[fig-66]]).

[[fig-67]] sweeps width across five penalty settings. Wider dictionaries do not only find more features; they find rarer ones, which the paper reads as evidence that a 512-neuron layer has not been exhausted.

One complication arrives from outside. [[external-replication|A researcher who trained his own autoencoder on a different one-layer model]] found more than half his features in an ultra-low cluster, almost all sharing a single encoder direction, which re-formed across random seeds and survived an attempt to train it away.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: What the assembled evidence licenses
chapters.body:
Set the training-run diagnostics aside and ask what the finished argument supports.

The paper's summary lists four lines of evidence: detailed proxies for a handful of features, blinded human scoring of a random sample, automated scoring of activations, and automated scoring of logit weights. None is decisive alone. The case is a conjunction, and the links are not equally strong.

The strongest one is structural and easy to miss. The autoencoder was fit to MLP activations and nothing else. What a feature does to the output — its [[logit-weight|effect on each next-token logit]] — was never an input to the fitting.

So [[downstream-effects-outside-dictionary-learning|when those effects turn out to match the activation story]], the agreement cannot be an artifact of the training procedure. It is the one place where the argument does not lean on a rubric the authors invented.

The remaining worry is [[model-vs-data-question|whether the features describe the model or only the dataset]]. The control is [[randomized-transformer|dictionary learning on a weight-shuffled copy of the same transformer]]. Shuffling within each matrix keeps the weight distributions identical, so anything recovered must come from the data.

It did not come out clean. On the automated activation score the randomized features take a slightly higher median than the real ones, which is what [[fig-70]] shows.

The paper's answer is to split the randomized features on whether they are [[single-token-features|driven by one token]]. Those are abundant in the shuffled model and trivially easy for a scorer to explain. On the remainder the real features win, and the shuffled ones score like polysemantic neurons.

That split is post-hoc, and the paper presents it as such rather than as a test passed.

What the rest supports is comparative. [[manual-interpretability-scoring|The blinded rater]] and [[automated-interpretability|the model-written explanations]] both place features far above neurons, on rubrics built to apply identically to each. Matched across two seeds, features agree at [[feature-vs-neuron-universality|a median 0.72 against the neurons' 0.46]]. In an outside replication, [[fig-63|92% of learned directions are spread across many neurons]].

Features beat neurons on every measure the paper built. That is not the same as the features being right.

chapters.title: What the paper says it does not have
chapters.body:
The authors' accounting of what they lack runs longer than their list of results.

Start with the headline number. [[loss-recovery-caveats|Two reasons are given not to lean on 79%]]. They expect a long tail of features, so each further percent of loss explained would need disproportionately more of them — which makes a percentage a doubtful unit for the question. And they do not believe the features are fully monosemantic; some polysemanticity may be sitting in low activations.

That meets a second problem from the scoring work. Interpretability falls off in the lower bands of a feature's activation range, and [[low-interval-activation-skew|most actual activations land in those bands]].

The defence is [[large-activations-dominate|that a feature's effect on the output is dominated by its strong firings]]. For the case-study features this is shown, by re-weighting the activation histogram by magnitude. For features in general, and for anything larger than this model, it is argued rather than measured.

A quieter caveat sits beside it. [[interpretability-importance-caveat|The scored features were sampled uniformly]], and interpretability might correlate with how important a feature is. The authors expect the important ones to look better, on the strength of inspection rather than an experiment.

Then there is the question of what a dictionary even is. [[feature-splitting|Widening the autoencoder divides existing features into finer ones]], so [[dictionary-resolution|the feature set is a setting rather than an answer]]. Asking how many features the layer holds has no reply at this stage.

And the whole result stands on one layer. Part of why that model was chosen is that a feature's effect on the logits is close to linear in its activation, which is what makes ablations and logit weights readable at all. More layers take that away.

The forward gaps are named directly. [[scaling-sparse-autoencoders|Applying the method to frontier models]] is called the most important question: a 100× expansion on a width-10,000 MLP is roughly 20 billion parameters, and rare features may demand a large slice of the big model's corpus, so the autoencoder could cost more to train than the model it reads. [[scaling-laws-for-dictionary-learning|The scaling relationships that would settle that do not exist]]. [[attentional-superposition|Attention layers are untouched]]. And [[scalability-of-analysis|turning feature-level detail into an understanding of a whole model]] would remain in the way even if superposition were solved outright.

n-the-unit-problem--the-counting-argumen.title: Why a layer would pack more than it holds
n-the-unit-problem--the-counting-argumen.intro: The parent gave the shape of the argument. This level walks the counting that sets the ceiling, the inversion problem sparsity has to solve before the packing is usable, the arithmetic of what overlap actually costs, and how much of each piece the paper shows rather than assumes.

chapters.title: Counting directions in 512 dimensions
chapters.body:
The layer is fixed. The MLP of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] has 512 ReLU neurons, and it sits on a [[residual-stream]] of only 128 dimensions. So the MLP is already four times wider than the stream it reads from and writes back into. Every activation vector this paper decomposes is a point in $\mathbb{R}^{512}$.

Now the counting. Give each property its own coordinate and you get 512 properties, full stop. Coordinates here are neurons, and neurons are a candidate unit at all only because the elementwise ReLU singles them out — a [[privileged-basis]].

Give each property its own direction instead: a unit vector $\mathbf{d}_i$ in the same space, which is the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]] taken literally, and in the trained dictionary is a column of the decoder ([[feature-direction]]). If you insist those directions be mutually orthogonal, the count is still 512. Orthogonality is the binding constraint, not the choice between coordinates and directions.

Relax it. Ask only that $|\mathbf{d}_i \cdot \mathbf{d}_j| \le \epsilon$ for some small $\epsilon$. The number of unit vectors meeting that condition in $\mathbb{R}^n$ grows exponentially in $n$ rather than linearly. That is standard high-dimensional geometry. The paper does not restate the bound, and it never names a value of $\epsilon$ it believes the trained model achieves.

What it does name is how wide it builds its own dictionary. [[table-1]] lists runs from 512 units ($1\times$) up to 131,072 ($256\times$), with the detailed analysis on 4,096 ($8\times$). That ratio is the [[expansion-factor]], and having more directions than dimensions is [[overcompleteness]] — the property the paper says separates its setting from ordinary factorization, and the reason this is [[dictionary-learning]].

Be clear what that width is. It is a hyperparameter the experimenters chose. It is not a measurement of how many features the layer carries in [[superposition]].

chapters.title: What sparsity has to buy
chapters.body:
Near-perpendicular packing is available in any high-dimensional space. Whether it is *usable* is a separate question, and it turns on reading the code back out.

Here is the inversion. Recovering feature activations $\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{4096}$ from an activation vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{512}$ means determining 4,096 numbers from 512 measurements. The system is underdetermined by a factor of eight. Infinitely many $\mathbf{f}$ reproduce any given $\mathbf{x}$ exactly.

Sparsity is what picks one out. If almost every entry of $\mathbf{f}$ is zero, the sparse solution can be unique even though the dense ones are not. That is [[compressed-sensing]], and the paper names it as the hard inner problem sitting inside its method.

So [[feature-sparsity]] is the load-bearing condition. Where does it come from? Not from measuring the transformer. The paper cites the long-standing hypothesis that the latent variables behind natural data are mostly inactive at any moment ([[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables]]), and says the language-model features anyone has seen so far are "suggestive of highly sparse variables". Suggestive is the paper's own word. The assumption is imported, then enforced by the training objective rather than checked against the model.

The condition also constrains what method is legitimate. Exact sparse recovery is NP-hard ([[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery]]). The transformer is certainly not solving an NP-hard problem when its own downstream components read these activations. So a decomposition strong enough to do exact recovery would be the wrong instrument: it could extract structure the model itself has no way to use.

The paper makes that argument explicitly and chooses a deliberately [[weak-dictionary-learning]] method on its strength — a [[sparse-autoencoder]], one ReLU layer up and one linear layer down, "similar in architecture to the MLP layers in language models". Established iterative solvers ([[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms]]) were tried and set aside, on that ground and on scaling.

Sparsity therefore does double duty: it makes the packing affordable for the model, and it makes the decomposition recoverable at all. [[l0-norm]] is the paper's later handle on how much of it the fit actually got.

chapters.title: Paying the tax, and finding it in the weights
chapters.body:
Nothing about the bargain is free, and it helps to see the size of the bill.

Take two feature directions with $\mathbf{d}_i \cdot \mathbf{d}_j = 0.1$. Suppose feature $j$ fires at activation 5 on some token. A readout aimed along $\mathbf{d}_i$ then collects $0.5$ of signal that belongs entirely to $j$. Now sum that over thousands of pairs. Sparsity holds most of those terms at zero on any given token, which is the whole point, but not all of them. The residue is [[interference]], and it is structural: the geometry keeps imposing it after training converges.

The dictionary pays it too. The paper reports that the encoder does not end up as the transpose of the decoder ([[untied-decoder-weights]]). Features with closely related dictionary vectors acquire encoder vectors tilted away from each other, so a nearly shared direction can still be read apart ([[encoder-decoder-offset-crosstalk]]). Untying was worth doing, which is a small piece of evidence that crosstalk is a live constraint inside the fit.

Where does the paper claim to see interference in the *model*? In the [[logit-weight]]. Push a feature's direction through the MLP output matrix $W_{down}$ ([[mlp-output-weights]]), a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding — [[path-expansion-logit-attribution]]. What comes out is one number per vocabulary token: how much that feature's firing moves that token's next-token logit.

For the [[arabic-script-feature]] the histogram ([[fig-10]]) has two humps. A fat one at approximately zero covering nearly the entire vocabulary, and a small one far to the right holding Arabic characters and the byte tokens \xd8 and \xd9 that begin their UTF-8 encodings ([[logit-weight-second-mode]]).

[[weight-interference]] is the paper's reading of the fat hump: weights the model would prefer at zero but cannot have there, because this feature's direction overlaps others whose weights it does want.

Hold that at arm's length. It is a hypothesis fitted to a shape. Softmax is shift-invariant, so logit weights have no absolute scale and each feature's distribution is centred at its own median ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]) — the main mode sits at zero partly by that construction, so the separation of the second mode is what carries the weight, not the position of the first. The paper's own cross-model comparison also offers a competing reading: the model may simply not care what a feature does to tokens that were already implausible. Nothing here separates forced noise from indifference.

chapters.title: How much of this was shown here
chapters.body:
Almost none of the mechanism above was established in this paper, and it is worth being exact about the provenance.

[[toy-models-of-superposition]] trained small ReLU networks to reconstruct synthetic inputs through a bottleneck. The inputs were sparse by construction, with sparsity a knob the experimenters turned. No language, no text, no transformer. What those models showed is that past a certain sparsity they stop allocating one bottleneck dimension per input and start packing.

[[noisy-simulation]] is that result restated as a claim about real networks, and [[fig-3]] is its picture: the layer you can inspect is a squeezed-down projection of a larger, sparser network you cannot. This paper reproduces the figure and reasons from it.

The inherited picture has a specific shape, which the paper later names the [[isotropic-superposition-model]]: features are discrete, one-dimensional, and repel each other through interference into a roughly even spread of directions. Two further imports sit beside it — [[polysemanticity-and-capacity]] for when a network prefers one representation over the other, and [[memorization-in-superposition]] for what happens on small repeated datasets.

None of this is re-derived. The paper assumes the picture and tests a consequence of it: if the layer is packed this way, an overcomplete sparse decomposition should recover interpretable pieces. Recovering them is evidence for the premise, but indirect evidence.

Then the assumption moves under its own results. In the discussion the authors say the inherited model was missing something ([[theories-of-superposition]]). Related feature directions do not spread evenly; they clump ([[feature-geometry-clusters]]), which the authors attribute more to features sharing downstream effects ([[action-sharing-features]]) than to their firing together ([[correlated-features]]). And features may not be one-dimensional intensities at all ([[feature-manifolds]]).

So the mechanism is assumed at the start and revised at the end. What it licenses in between is a choice among [[three-approaches-to-superposition]]: decode a model that has superposition, rather than try to build one that does not.

n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ab.title: The route that was abandoned, and what was on it
n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ab.intro: The parent named four things on this route. This level says what each one actually did: the mechanism SoLU used and the column the earlier paper did not print, what the equal-loss claim rested on and how it came apart, the four-feature calculation that ended the authors' own attempts, and how a neighbouring literature arrives at the same methods with the opposite count.

chapters.title: What SoLU bought, and the column it did not print
chapters.body:
Start with why the neuron basis is special at all.

An MLP's nonlinearity is applied one coordinate at a time. Rotate the coordinate system and the function changes, because a ReLU applied to a rotated vector is not the rotation of the ReLU applied to the original. The architecture therefore singles out the neuron axes. They are a [[privileged-basis]], and no other set of axes has that status.

This is the reason anyone expected to read a layer neuron by neuron in the first place. It is also weaker than it sounds. A privileged basis gives a [[feature-direction]] a tendency to sit near an axis; it does not make it sit on one. A replication comment in this paper measures the gap on the model studied here: 92% of dictionary directions are dense in the neuron basis, and yet [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test|the heavy tail of those weights]] still says the basis is privileged.

[[solu]] tried to turn the tendency into a pressure. Its activation function suppresses everything but a few large entries, so a feature spread thinly across many neurons is hard to express, while a feature carried by one large neuron is cheap. Training then has a reason to push features onto axes, and [[monosemanticity]] becomes something the architecture rewards rather than something you hope for.

The reported gain was a count: more neurons a person could read.

This paper supplies the other column, and keeps its hedge. Training with SoLU *appears* to make some neurons more interpretable at the cost of making others less interpretable than before. No net figure is given.

There is a second wrinkle in how the gain was counted. Section 4.1 names the authors' own SoLU work as the prior work that judged units mainly by [[top-dataset-examples]] — the handful of inputs where a unit fires hardest. Many [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] units look clean from the top and stop looking clean further down, which the paper calls [[max-dataset-example-bias]].

What SoLU did leave is concrete units. A base64 neuron, a hexadecimal neuron and an all-caps neuron were found there, and [[solu-base64-neuron|the base64 one]] returns in this paper as evidence about [[universality]].

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

chapters.title: Minima at the same loss, and the loss function that allowed them
chapters.body:
The second published piece offered something SoLU did not: the possibility that readability was free.

[[engineering-monosemanticity]] trained MLP layers on a [[compressed-sensing]] task — many signals, only a few of them active at once, packed into fewer dimensions than there are signals and then recovered. That [[feature-sparsity|few-at-a-time property]] is what makes the packing possible. The layer is fit by squared error against the signals it is meant to reconstruct.

Run the fit repeatedly and you do not get one solution. Jermyn et al. found several minima sitting at the same loss. Some were strongly polysemantic. Some were strongly monosemantic.

Read the shape of that result rather than the result itself. If two solutions cost the same, there is no performance argument for the unreadable one. Nothing would need redesigning. A training intervention — an initialization, a schedule, a nudge — could steer a run into the readable basin, and you would pay nothing for the steering.

[[mse-loss-and-monosemanticity|Why squared error permits this]] is the crux. MSE scores a reconstruction against a target and is indifferent to the code used to reach it; two encodings with equal error are equally good. Scherlis et al. push further, showing that for some feature importance curves an MSE model actively prefers the monosemantic arrangement, within [[polysemanticity-and-capacity|a framework for when a network wants which]].

Two things then withdrew the offer.

Later work on more realistic tasks found the equal-loss property was specific to the task chosen. The paper reports this in a single sentence and points at no run, so the reader takes it on the authors' word.

The second objection is not about the task. Language models are not trained with squared error, and nothing about the geometry of MSE minima has to survive the move to cross-entropy over next tokens.

The same argument cuts favourably once. The autoencoder this paper trains is fit with [[mse-reconstruction-term|an MSE term]] plus [[l1-sparsity-penalty|an L1 penalty]], which is why the authors think the dictionary will not hide features in superposition itself — the worry they call [[superposition-all-the-way-down]].

chapters.title: Out to one-hot, and still polysemantic
chapters.body:
The paper's own attempts get one paragraph in section 2.3 and one line in the author contributions. There are no plots.

What was tried was [[activation-sparsity-training]]: pushing the subject model toward few active neurons, out to the limit of one-hot activations where exactly one neuron is on. At that limit the [[l0-norm|number of nonzero activations]] is 1. Superposition is then impossible by construction, and there is no [[interference]] left to worry about, because you cannot pack more directions into a layer than it has neurons when only one coordinate is ever nonzero.

It worked in that narrow sense. The contributions section credits Brian Chen with building models whose neurons typically activated in isolation, and then showing those neurons were still polysemantic.

He then produced the counter-example that explains why.

Take one neuron with a binary output and four mutually exclusive [[feature|features]] A, B, C, D, each equally likely and each predicting its own next token.

Let the neuron fire on A alone and predict A correctly. A quarter of the time it is right at no cost. The other three quarters it stays silent and the model guesses uniformly among B, C and D, paying $\ln 3 \approx 1.10$ each time. The average is $\tfrac{3}{4}\ln 3 \approx 0.82$.

Now let it fire on A and B together, predicting a coin flip between their two tokens. Half the time it fires and pays $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$. The other half it is silent and the model splits between C and D, paying $\ln 2$ again. The average is $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$.

The ambiguous neuron wins by roughly $0.13$ nats. [[cross-entropy-favors-polysemanticity|Under cross-entropy]], holding two features vaguely beats holding one cleanly and discarding the rest.

The argument does not rest on the model having a single neuron. At the sparsity limit only one neuron fires at a time, so you can always take that neuron and the cases where it fires, and the same trade is on offer there.

This is [[polysemanticity-without-superposition]], and it is what moves [[architectural-approaches-to-superposition|the verdict]] from expensive to non-viable. Removing superposition does not remove polysemanticity. They were two problems under one name.

chapters.title: Disentanglement wants a different number
chapters.body:
[[disentanglement]] is a separate literature, and the paper's reason for placing it beside the architectural attempts is that its methods are the same kind of thing: change the architecture or the objective so the representation comes out readable.

The difference is a count.

Disentanglement looks for a representation whose dimensions separate the [[factors-of-variation]] behind the data — the conceptually distinct influences that generated it. The target number of factors is typically the dimension of the space. One axis, one factor.

[[superposition]] asks for more features than there are dimensions. That is [[overcompleteness]], and the paper treats it as the thing that separates its setting from this whole tradition.

The three methods it names all act at training time. Kim and Mnih push a variational autoencoder to disentangle by encouraging independence across its latent dimensions. Chen et al. do it inside a GAN by maximizing the mutual information between a small subset of factors and the data. Makhzani and Frey use a [[topk-activation]], keeping the $k$ largest hidden units and zeroing the rest.

Read that way, SoLU is a disentangling method too.

Here the paper makes its sharpest claim about the family. [[disentanglement-vs-superposition|Disentangling pressure, it says, typically hurts performance]], because succeeding would mean throwing away features the model has reasons to keep. So the model does not comply. It responds by entangling the features that survive more strongly than before.

The support is two results in different settings: Mahinpei et al., and the authors' own SoLU finding that some neurons became harder to read. Two data points offered as a pattern, not as a demonstration.

Notice what is not being rejected. The paper's own [[sparse-autoencoder]] runs on exactly this kind of sparsity pressure. The objection was never to sparsity as a tool. It was to imposing it on the model under study rather than on a [[dictionary-learning|dictionary fitted to that model afterwards]].

n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ho.title: How Strong the Solver Is Allowed to Be
n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ho.intro: The parent gave the shape of the argument: the inner problem is hard, the classical solvers were dropped, and an autoencoder took their place for two stated reasons. This level does the arithmetic behind "hard", says what the classical methods actually compute, puts numbers on the scale claim, and separates the parts of the weak-solver argument that are demonstrated from the parts that are asserted.

chapters.title: 512 equations, 4,096 unknowns
chapters.body:
Fix the dictionary for a moment. Suppose the directions are already known, and the only thing left is to compute how strongly each one fires on a given token.

That is the inner problem. [[linear-feature-decomposition|The decomposition]] states it as $\mathbf{x} \approx \mathbf{b} + \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{d}_i$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is the activation vector of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|512-neuron layer]], each $\mathbf{d}_i$ is a [[feature-direction|unit direction]] and each $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ is the [[feature-activation|coefficient]] to be found.

Count what you have. Each of the 512 coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ gives one linear equation. There are 4,096 unknowns. The solutions therefore form an affine subspace of dimension $4096 - 512 = 3584$.

This is not underdetermined by a little. Fixing $\mathbf{x}$ leaves a 3,584-dimensional space of coefficient vectors, every one of which reconstructs it exactly.

Now add sparsity. Choose a support — a set of $k$ coefficients allowed to be nonzero — and the corresponding $k$ columns of [[dictionary-decoder|the dictionary]] span a $k$-dimensional subspace. When $k$ is far below 512 and the columns sit in general position, $\mathbf{x}$ lies in that small subspace only for the one support that generated it, and other supports miss.

Uniqueness comes back by ruling out almost every support, not by adding equations. The paper asserts this rather than deriving it: sparsity, it says, is the only thing that makes the problem possible at all. This is [[compressed-sensing]].

The overlap runs the other way too. You cannot place 4,096 mutually perpendicular unit vectors in 512 dimensions, so the columns have nonzero dot products with one another, and reading off one coefficient by projection picks up contributions from every other active feature — [[interference]]. [[noisy-simulation|The paper's picture of superposition]] has the transformer itself living with that cross-talk.

Earlier transformer work that recovered an [[undercomplete-basis|undercomplete basis]] never met this. With 512 directions or fewer, least squares answers the inner problem outright.

chapters.title: What the classical solvers actually compute
chapters.body:
The hardness result is narrower than it sounds. What is [[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery|NP-hard]] is exact recovery: finding the genuinely sparsest coefficient vector consistent with the activation.

Written out, that is minimising the $L^0$ count of nonzeros, which is a combinatorial search over supports. If ten features fire on a token, the honest version of the search considers every choice of ten columns out of 4,096. Nobody runs that.

So the field does not run it. [[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms|The established methods]] take one of two routes around the wall, and the paper names both: relax the problem, or search greedily.

Relaxing means replacing the nonzero count with something convex. [[l1-sparsity-penalty|An $L^1$ penalty]] on the coefficients is the usual substitute, since it is a sum rather than a count and still drives most coordinates to exactly zero. Greedy search means matching pursuit: pick the column most correlated with the current residual, add it, re-fit the coefficients, subtract, repeat.

Method of Optimal Directions and K-SVD wrap either of those in an outer loop. Hold the dictionary fixed and run the sparse coding step on every datapoint; then hold the codes fixed and update the dictionary — MOD by one least-squares solve for the whole matrix, K-SVD one column at a time via a small singular value decomposition, revising the active coefficients as it goes.

Note what alternation implies. Every outer iteration touches every datapoint, and each touch runs a search.

The paper's report on trying these is one clause long: it tried several, and moved on. No run is described, no metric is quoted, no failure is characterised. Given that the authors elsewhere say they have [[recognizing-good-features|no systematic way]] to tell a good dictionary from a bad one, and fall back on [[manual-inspection|looking at features]], a decisive comparison would have been hard to adjudicate even if one had been run.

chapters.title: Eight billion activation vectors, each seen once
chapters.body:
The first stated reason is scale, and the training setup gives it a size.

The transformer is run over 40 million contexts from [[pile-dataset|the Pile]], and the MLP activation vector after the ReLU is collected for every token. From each context, 250 of those vectors are kept, then shuffled together with vectors from other contexts so that a batch spans many documents — [[activation-shuffling|cross-context shuffling]]. That yields [[autoencoder-training-dataset|about 10 billion activation vectors]].

Training uses just over 8 billion of them. The batch size is 8,192 and there are 1 million update steps, which multiply to roughly 8.2 billion — one vector per slot, [[sampling-without-replacement|with no vector seen twice]]. The paper says not repeating data matters for good results.

Hold that against the alternating loop. An iterative method wants repeated passes over a stored data matrix, and each pass runs a per-datapoint search. Eight billion pursuits per outer iteration, several outer iterations deep, is a different order of cost from eight billion forward-backward passes taken once.

The autoencoder also keeps [[extended-training-steps|running long after the loss plateaus]], alongside [[learning-rate-sweep|a sweep of learning rates]] and [[neuron-resampling|periodic revival of dead hidden units]] — none of which has an obvious counterpart in a solver that terminates when its inner search converges.

What the extra data is claimed to buy is stated carefully. More data made features subjectively sharper and more interpretable. That is the authors reading examples, not a curve; no measurement of sharpness against dataset size is reported.

The same pressure is where the method's future difficulty sits. [[scaling-sparse-autoencoders|Applied to a frontier model]], a 100x expansion on a width-10,000 layer would be a 20-billion-parameter autoencoder, and rare features may demand a large fraction of the subject model's own corpus. [[scaling-laws-for-dictionary-learning|How those requirements grow]] is not known.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

chapters.title: One matrix multiply per token
chapters.body:
The second reason is the interesting one, because it argues for a limitation rather than against it.

Here is the whole solver. [[autoencoder-encoder|The encoder]] computes $\mathbf{f} = \text{ReLU}(W_e(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d) + \mathbf{b}_e)$: subtract a bias, apply one matrix, add another bias, clip at zero. No residual, no second pass, no look at which other coefficients came out large.

That shape is the point. It is the same shape as the MLP layer whose activations it is reading, which is the paper's stated ground for expecting it to be similarly able to pull features out of superposition — no more able, and no less.

The search has not vanished; it has moved. [[amortized-sparse-coding-approximation|The paper calls the encoder an amortized, linear approximation to a multi-step, non-linear sparse coding algorithm]] — the cost is paid once during training, in the weights, and each token then gets a single-shot answer.

One visible consequence. Because the encoder cannot condition on context, it has to absorb interference into fixed weights, and [[untied-decoder-weights|the paper's decision not to tie encoder to decoder]] is where that shows. [[base64-feature-family|The three base64 features]] have closely related dictionary vectors, but their encoder vectors are [[encoder-decoder-offset-crosstalk|tilted further apart]] than the transpose would allow, which the paper reads as preventing one from firing on another's input.

Two limits on the argument are worth keeping straight.

First, the weakness constraint binds the per-token readout only. The dictionary itself was found by gradient descent over 8 billion datapoints, which is not a weak procedure — the claim is about what can be recovered at inference, not about how the directions were located.

Second, no comparison is reported. Nothing shows a stronger solver surfacing structure the transformer cannot use. [[weak-dictionary-learning|The concern]] is stated, acted on, and left untested.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: Where the sparsity assumption came from
chapters.body:
Everything above rests on one premise that the paper does not establish: that the true coefficients are sparse in the first place.

Its source is named. [[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables|A long-standing hypothesis]] holds that the latent variables generating natural data are mostly inactive at any moment, and the paper cites Olshausen and Field's "Why Sparseness?" for it directly.

The supporting evidence from language models is thin, and the paper says so. It grants a limited understanding of what features exist in these models, and calls the examples it has suggestive. [[toy-models-of-superposition|Its own earlier toy work]] supplies the other half: that a large set of sparse features can be carried as directions in a lower-dimensional space.

The method has a lineage too. [[prior-dictionary-learning-on-embeddings|Sparse coding was applied to word embeddings years earlier]] — by Faruqui et al. and Arora et al. with sparse coding, by Subramanian et al. with a [[sparse-autoencoder]], by Zhang et al. with [[dictionary-learning]] proper, and by Panigrahi et al. with Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Yun et al. brought dictionary learning to a 12-layer transformer's residual stream, but recovered fewer directions than dimensions.

A neighbouring literature is explicitly not the same thing. [[disentanglement|Disentanglement]] looks for representations whose dimensions separate [[factors-of-variation|distinct influences on the data]], typically as many factors as there are dimensions — including [[topk-activation|hard sparsity by keeping the top $k$ activations]]. Overcompleteness is what the paper says makes its setting different, and [[disentanglement-vs-superposition|it expects disentangling interventions to hurt]], since succeeding would mean discarding features.

And the approach was not being tried alone. [[cunningham-et-al-parallel-work|A parallel line of interim reports]], prompted by the same toy-models paper, was running sparse autoencoders on one-layer transformers at the same time.

n-the-model-and-the-tool--the-objective.title: The four lines, and the arguments inside them
n-the-model-and-the-tool--the-objective.intro: The parent showed the four lines whole. This node reads them in order — what the first line ties together, what the encoder and the decoder each are as matrices — and then takes the three design choices sitting inside them one at a time, with the evidence the paper actually offers for each.

chapters.title: The line that runs before anything is learned
chapters.body:
The first of [[eq-autoencoder-loss|the four lines]] does nothing that looks like learning:

$$\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$$

One fixed vector is subtracted from every activation before the encoder sees it.

The subscript is the whole point. $\mathbf{b}_d$ is the decoder's output bias — the same vector added back on the third line. The paper ties the two: one learned parameter, subtracted at the input and restored at the output, rather than two independent biases. Used on the input side it is a [[pre-encoder-bias]].

So the autoencoder works in coordinates centred on $\mathbf{b}_d$, and undoes the shift when it writes its answer.

That makes the fit an instance of the decomposition the paper set up earlier, $\mathbf{x} \approx \mathbf{b} + \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{d}_i$ — [[eq-feature-decomposition]] — with $\mathbf{b}_d$ playing the part of $\mathbf{b}$. Every activation is one fixed offset plus a sparse combination of [[feature-direction|feature directions]].

The reason given is a toy-model result. Without a learned bias at both ends, the authors report the autoencoder failed to reproduce [[bounce-plots]], a diagnostic they had used on synthetic problems where the right answer is known. The tied bias is initialized to [[geometric-median-initialization|the geometric median]] of the activation dataset, the point minimizing summed distance to all datapoints.

The appendix ranks this first among its six modifications, roughly by importance.

It also states, before listing any of them, that the modifications appeared at different times and interact, so no rigorous ablations are supplied — intuition and anecdotal evidence instead. That caveat covers everything in this chapter and the two that follow.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: One readout, then one write
chapters.body:
The second line is the encoder — [[eq-encoder]]:

$$\mathbf{f} = \text{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$$

With $n$ the input dimension and $m$ the hidden width, $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$. Here $n = 512$, the width of the MLP layer whose activations are the target ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

Read it row by row. Row $i$ of $W_e$ is one direction in activation space. Dot it with the centred activation, add the scalar $b_{e,i}$, apply ReLU. Out comes one non-negative number, the activation of feature $i$ — [[feature-activation]]. Doing that $m$ times in parallel is the entire [[autoencoder-encoder|encoder]].

The ReLU is what lets the sparsity penalty bite. It returns exact zeros, not small numbers, so a feature that is off contributes nothing at all to the reconstruction and nothing to the penalty.

The third line is the decoder:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_d\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{b}_d$$

The columns of $W_d \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ are the dictionary — the paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" for the same matrix ([[dictionary-decoder]]). Reconstruction is a weighted sum of columns, with $\mathbf{f}$ supplying the weights, and most weights zero.

The hidden layer is wider than the input, $m \geq n$. That is [[overcompleteness]], and the ratio $m/n$ is the [[expansion-factor]].

Notice what is absent between the two lines. No second hidden layer, no nonlinearity in the decoder, no iteration, no search. Weights start from [[kaiming-uniform-initialization|PyTorch's default initialization]].
