n-what-the-collection-looks-like--featur.title: Every feature is also a move
n-what-the-collection-looks-like--featur.intro: The parent handed you the list of machines. This level takes them one at a time, and starts with the thing that decides how much any of them is worth: what an arrow in these diagrams actually is, and what the paper measured in order to draw one.

chapters.title: What an arrow actually is
chapters.body:
The arrows in every diagram in this section are not weights.

The paper studies a [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. Two features living in the same MLP have no path to each other inside one forward pass: the MLP runs once, its output joins the residual stream, and the residual stream goes to the logits. Nothing downstream of the MLP feeds back into it.

So the route from one feature to the next is longer than a wire. A [[feature]] fires. Its [[logit-weight]] vector — the [[feature-direction]] pushed through the [[mlp-output-weights]], a linearised layer norm, and the [[unembedding-matrix]] — raises the next-token logits for some set of tokens. The model samples one of them. That token is embedded at the next position, and there it switches on a second feature.

The handoff leaves the network, becomes text, and comes back in. That is the whole of what [[finite-state-automata-features]] means here, and it is why the paper says these assemblies are not [[circuit]]s.

A circuit is a subgraph of the computation, held together by weights. These are held together by the dataset. The paper's footnote is precise about the difference: the model never learned these features to work together. It learned each one separately while fitting text, and they line up because real text has the shapes it has. A model trained with reinforcement learning, the paper adds, might have systems of this kind that genuinely co-adapted during training. This one does not.

Notice what the evidence is, before the machines get interesting. Each box is a strip of [[top-dataset-examples]], shaded by activation ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). Each arrow label is the top of a ranked logit-weight list, printed without magnitudes.

No sampled continuations. No ablations. No measured transition rates.

Every arrow is one claim: these tokens rank high on that feature's list, and those tokens fall inside this other feature's firing set. It is a reading of two lists laid side by side. Reading a feature by what it promotes rather than by what it detects is the [[action-features]] move, and the entire section rests on it.

chapters.title: One node, then two
chapters.body:
[[fig-55]] is four panels that have nothing to do with each other. Each is a single box with one arrow leaving it and coming straight back in: A/0/45 base64, A/0/489 uppercase DNA ([[dna-feature]]), A/0/14 French, A/0/209 SQL. All four are [[context-features]] — on across a stretch of text of one kind, rather than on one word.

Walk the base64 panel to see why the arrow closes. The paper models base64 as roughly uniform draws from a 64-symbol alphabet, six bits a character, so its two-character fragments look like nothing else in the corpus. The tokens A/0/45 promotes are Qg, zA, YW, MQ. Sample one of those and the text at the next position is still base64. The feature fires again — on a token it helped put there.

Nothing about this is special to base64. Any context feature whose promoted tokens are diagnostic of its own context will loop ([[self-exciting-feature-loop]]). The figure prints thirteen such tokens for base64 and six for SQL, top-of-list in both cases.

Everything here comes from run A/0: 512 features for a 512-dimensional MLP activation space, an [[expansion-factor]] of one. The dictionary is not [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]], and the paper gives that as the reason these pictures stay this small. The A/0–A/5 sequence holds the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] fixed and grows the dictionary ([[dictionary-learning-run]]); by A/1's 4,096 features the single [[base64-feature]] has already become three ([[feature-splitting]]).

[[fig-56]] adds a node, and one more arrow than you would expect. A/0/207 fires on all-caps word pieces — BOT, TAC, the SPA in SPACER. A/0/358 fires on the underscores between them. Under the paper's [[feature-notation]] both read as model A, run 0, then an index.

There are three arrows, not two. A/0/207 loops back to itself on nine caps continuations, and separately promotes "_". A/0/358 promotes ten openings of fresh caps segments — MEM, MAX, END, BEGIN — back into 207.

So the self-loop is what lets a segment run long, and the underscore edge is what ends it. Alternate them: ARRAY_MAX_VALUE.

chapters.title: Machines the tokenizer forces
chapters.body:
The next pair of machines exist because of the tokenizer.

The vocabulary comes from [[byte-pair-encoding]] over bytes, so a non-Latin character often arrives as several tokens ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]). Take Tamil ண, code point U+0BA3. Its UTF-8 encoding is the three bytes E0 AE A3. The tokenizer has merged the first two into one token, `\xe0\xae`, and leaves `\xa3` standing alone.

Call those the prefix and the suffix. The prefix roughly fixes which Unicode block the character sits in. The suffix picks the character inside that block.

The alternation is then forced by the encoding. A prefix can only be followed by a continuation byte. A suffix completes a character, so a fresh one can start.

[[fig-57]]'s left panel is exactly that. A/1/2499 fires on suffix bytes, and its top logit weights are `\xe0\xae` and `\xe0\xaf`. A/1/522 fires on those prefixes, and its top logit weights are continuation bytes. Two nodes, two arrows, alternating ([[unicode-token-state-machines]]).

One number is worth pausing on. The Tamil block runs U+0B80–U+0BFF, 128 code points, and those two prefix tokens cover all of it. So A/1/2499's arrow label is not a truncated top-of-list — it is the complete set. The same tokenizer fact shapes where the paper's [[arabic-script-feature]] fires and what it predicts.

Note also that this pair comes from A/1, not A/0. It survived a round of splitting.

Chinese breaks the symmetry, and the handling of it is the interesting part. Common characters get a dedicated token; rarer ones split. The paper's observation is that a complete character occupies the same slot as a suffix — either can be followed by a whole new character, or by a new prefix.

So the [[sparse-autoencoder]] gives both cases to one feature. A/0/397 fires on complete characters and on suffix bytes, and its logit weights fall into two groups, drawn as two arrows. Whole-character tokens — 是, 的, 在 — loop back into itself. Prefix tokens go to A/0/101, which fires only on prefixes and predicts suffixes, returning to 397.

Two nodes, three arrows, and the shape is a fact about the encoding rather than about Chinese.

chapters.title: Four nodes, and one it cannot reach
chapters.body:
[[fig-58]] is the section's largest tidy machine ([[html-feature-automaton]]). A/0/20 fires on the bracket that opens a tag and promotes tag names: div, td, span, li, tr, thead, tbody, section, table. A/0/0 fires on tag names, hardest on ul, and promotes closes. A/0/30 fires on the close and promotes a newline followed by indentation. A/0/494 fires on that whitespace token and promotes ` <`, ` </`, ` <!--`, which lands back on A/0/20.

Run the cycle once and you get `<div>\n\t\t<span>`.

Now count the arrows: seven, not four. Two are shortcuts. A/0/0 and A/0/30 also promote tokens like `></` and `><`, which close one tag and open the next inside a single token, skipping the whitespace state. The tokenizer is making edges again.

One arrow is dashed and leaves the picture entirely. A/0/0 also promotes ` xmlns`, ` href`, ` class`. If the model emits an attribute name, nothing in these four features says what follows — the quote, the value, the closing quote, possibly further attributes. The paper points at this gap itself rather than leaving it for a reader to find.

That is the sharper form of its caution. The machine is not merely coarse because A/0 is small. It is incomplete on its own terms, at a state it can plainly reach.

[[fig-59]] is the contrast. Four A/0 features cover one IRC line: A/0/178 on the `<` that opens a nickname after a line break, A/0/153 across the nickname's interior, A/0/151 on the closing `>`, A/0/46 across the message body. Five arrows, two of them self-loops — 153 promotes more nick fragments so a handle can run to any length, 46 promotes " ubuntu", " linux", " sudo", " :)" so a message can.

The collision is the point. `<` and `>` are the same characters that drive the HTML machine, and different features claim them here. Token identity does not select the feature; position inside the line format does. That is the work [[token-in-context-features]] are doing.

The Ubuntu vocabulary is a fact about the corpus, which the paper presumes carries a great deal of Linux IRC ([[pile-dataset]]). Every feature named here can be looked up in the published [[feature-exploration-interface]].

chapters.title: A phrase with its own machine
chapters.body:
[[fig-60]] leaves A/0 behind. Its three features come from run A/4, and their indices are 11432, 58888 and 56745 — five digits, a dictionary in the tens of thousands.

A/4/11432 fires on the "A" in "…FITNESS FOR A" and promotes " PARTICULAR". A/4/58888 fires on " PARTICULAR" and promotes " PURPOSE". A/4/56745 fires on " PURPOSE". Three boxes, two arrows, no loop: the chain stops because the phrase stops.

The states have changed kind. Every earlier machine had a context for a state — base64 text, all-caps identifiers, a Unicode block, an IRC field. Here each state is a position inside one specific string.

The paper calls these [[memorization-features]] and says they appear only in runs with many features. A small dictionary spends its budget on broad contexts instead.

The family resemblance is to [[trigram-features]], which implement a short fixed continuation — predicting "19" after "COVID-". This is that, three times in a row.

Several readings are then offered and none of them closed. The paper ties the chain to [[memorization-in-superposition]], a prior finding that toy models trained on small repeated datasets memorize the datapoints in superposition rather than learning a rule that generalises. It also offers the chain as an instance of [[mechanistic-anomaly-detection]]: the model behaves differently in one narrow, specific case, and here you can name the units that make it do so.

Then it says it is surprising that anything this narrow fits inside a model with 512 neurons at all, and reads that as a demonstration of how much [[superposition]] can embed in few dimensions.

And then it takes some of that back. Because mechanisms like this are buried deep in superposition, the paper says, they are likely very noisy.

The corpus deserves the last word. This wording sits in the file headers of popular open-source licences, and the model saw 100 billion tokens of [[pile-dataset|the Pile]]. Heavy repetition is the stated reason the chain exists at all — which is [[model-vs-data-question]] in miniature, since a feature this specific may be tracking a quirk of the training text more than any computation.

n-what-the-collection-looks-like--wideni.title: Widening the dictionary, one feature at a time
n-what-the-collection-looks-like--wideni.intro: The parent gave the findings. This level is about how they were reached: what made a feature look like a bug in the first place, which of the base64 distinctions rest on a measurement and which rest on reading examples, and what the one measure the paper defines for linking runs actually does.

chapters.title: A slot spent on something the bigrams already knew
chapters.body:
The argument for calling the P feature a bug is an argument about capacity, and it is worth stating precisely.

In [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|the transformer under study]], the token embedding and the unembedding already form a path from the current token straight to the output logits. That path can carry any bigram statistics you like — the distribution over next tokens given the present one — with no MLP involvement at all. So a feature in [[mlp-activations-as-target|the layer being decomposed]] that fires on every instance of one token, at high magnitude, and does nothing more, is paying for something the model gets free elsewhere.

The coarse runs produce many of these. The paper's example fires on the token " P", and specifically on words where P is the first token, as in [ P][attern].

Two things made this more than an aesthetic complaint. [[single-token-features]] — where the same token carries the largest activation in all twenty of the sampled top examples — are abundant in a control transformer with randomized weights, and trivially easy to write an explanation for. And an independent report applying [[dictionary-learning]] to the residual stream had noticed the same preponderance.

[[fig-47]] is the resolution of the single blur. Widen the dictionary and that one feature becomes sixteen or more P features, each firing on P in a different context, with correspondingly different neuron activations and different logits. What looked like one detector was a family the coarse run could not separate.

One cost to record. The paper says these refined P features were found by [[manual-inspection]], not by any similarity computation. So this case of [[feature-splitting]] is an eyeball match across runs, closer to the paper's [[trigram-features|motif inventory]] than to a measurement.

chapters.title: The digits the base64 feature skipped
chapters.body:
The trio was not found by going looking for it. It was already sitting in the specificity evidence as an unexplained hole.

[[fig-25]], the earlier figure for [[base64-feature|A/1/2357]], stacks sampled tokens by activation level and colours each by a [[computational-proxy]]. Inside its base64 strings a few tokens sit at zero. They are the digits 2, 4, 7 and 9. The feature runs across base64 and skips lone digits within it.

The proxy cannot account for that. It models base64 as random draws from [a-zA-Z0-9+/], so those digits score as base64 like everything around them. Its Pearson correlation with the feature's activation is only 0.38, which the paper puts down to the proxy being too broad — hexadecimal strings score high on it too.

Now the coarse run. A/0 has 512 features, the same as the number of MLP neurons, so it is [[overcompleteness|not overcomplete]] at all. Its A/0/45 fires on every token of a base64 string, and it is also the feature matching the base64 neuron reported earlier in a SoLU model.

[[fig-48]] sets A/0/45's activations beside the three A/1 features. The paper's wording is that the three "seem to jointly cover" it. That is read off dataset examples. No coverage fraction is computed.

[[fig-49]] does the comparison that separates the first two. Both push up largely the same tokens — for a base64 feature these live in [[logit-weight-second-mode|the far-right mode]] of the [[logit-weight]] histogram, the base64-specific tokens rather than the bulk near zero. The exception is the ten digit tokens, which the digit feature holds down.

chapters.title: A distinction made by the tokenizer
chapters.body:
Walk the tokenizer, because the whole explanation lives there.

Byte-pair encoding builds its vocabulary by repeatedly merging frequent character pairs. Digit pairs are frequent in ordinary text, so common two-digit strings exist as single tokens. Tokenizing a base64 blob then proceeds greedily over the same vocabulary.

So consider two adjacent digits inside a base64 string. The merged token wins: [Bq][8][9][mp] is not a tokenization the model ever sees, because it comes out as [Bq][89][mp].

A lone digit token therefore carries information. It was not merged with what came after it, so what came after it is not a digit that would have merged with it.

That regularity is a property of the encoding, not of base64. Base64 output is close to uniform over its 64 characters, so in the underlying string a digit is no less likely after a digit than anywhere else. The pattern exists only once the string has been cut into tokens. The [[base64-digit-feature|digit feature]] suppressing digit logits is a correct prediction that earns loss.

How strong is this? The paper says it believes the behaviour is "likely an artifact" of tokenization. There is no experiment. The evidence is the non-occurrence of [Bq][8][9][mp], plus the reasoning above.

The consequence is a caution about reading splits. When a wider dictionary divides a [[context-features|context feature]], the new boundary need not be a boundary in the world; here it is a boundary in the input encoding, and the split alone does not say which. If the model does represent the regularity, it belongs among the [[true-features]] rather than counting as a defect — this is the [[model-vs-data-question]] arriving one layer lower down.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

chapters.title: Six spaces, and how thin the case is
chapters.body:
A/1/1544 had no rule visible in its examples. The break came from noticing one token it responds to particularly strongly: ICAgICAg, which decodes to six spaces in a row. Six spaces is indentation, and indentation only appears if the encoded bytes are text.

Turning that hunch into a check runs into an alignment problem. Base64 encodes three bytes as four characters, so decoding is only meaningful on four-character groups aligned with the start of the encoding. A substring cut at an arbitrary offset decodes to noise even when the full string is readable text.

The paper's procedure is to select substrings which, decoded with Python's base64 library, contain the maximal number of printable ASCII characters. That is a search over cuts, chosen so as not to miss text through misalignment.

[[fig-50]] is the result: top examples for A/1/1544 contain substrings that decode to ASCII, while none of the top examples for the other two do.

Weigh what that is. It is a contrast between three sets of top-activating dataset examples, drawn from [[activation-visualization-sampling|a 100-million-token subset]] through [[feature-exploration-interface|the published browser]]. The paper spends a whole section elsewhere on [[max-dataset-example-bias|why top examples flatter a unit]], and built its rubric to sample across activation bands for exactly that reason.

Here there is no proxy, no correlation number, and no look at what the feature does lower down its activation range. The [[activation-specificity|specificity]] apparatus the paper assembled for its four case studies is not applied. This is the paper's most worked example of [[multiple-features-for-one-context]], and its evidence is a reading of examples.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

chapters.title: One number for linking two dictionaries
chapters.body:
To claim a feature in one run refines a feature in another you need to say which pairs go together, and [[masked-cosine-similarity]] is the paper's answer.

Fix one feature from each run. Over sampled tokens each is a vector of activations, almost all zero. Let $S_a$ be the tokens where the first fires and $S_b$ the tokens where the second fires. Compute the cosine similarity of the two activation vectors restricted to $S_a$, then again restricted to $S_b$, and keep the larger of the two.

The masking is doing specific work. Splitting is containment: a fine feature covers part of a coarse feature's territory. Restricted to the fine feature's tokens the two track each other closely. Restricted to the coarse feature's tokens the fine one is zero across most of them and the similarity falls away. A single symmetric score over all tokens would rate the exact relationship being searched for as a weak match. Taking the greater of the two masks makes it a test for containment in either direction.

Two choices are stated plainly. Edges are drawn above about 0.4, a threshold picked to keep the graph small enough to visualize while still showing some richness. And [[ultralow-density-cluster|features firing on under one token in a million]] are dropped — 292 of A/1's 4,096, which the paper treats as a training artifact.

[[fig-46]] draws the survivors as a [[feature-relationship-graph]] across three widths. The finer runs separate the from a, which are followed by slightly different noun phrases: [[token-in-context-features]] splitting by grammar rather than topic.

And the graph both branches and rejoins, so [[splitting-is-not-a-tree]] — [[dictionary-resolution|zoom levels]], not a hierarchy you can walk.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--densi.title: The histogram you check first
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--densi.intro: The parent gave you the shape of the diagnostic. This level walks it as the authors use it: what exactly gets counted, what the three numbers are for, why the ultralow mode is read as something training produced rather than something the transformer contains, and what happens when the picture stops separating.

chapters.title: What the number actually counts
chapters.body:
Start with why counting is even well defined. The autoencoder's hidden layer is a ReLU layer, and the training objective adds an [[l1-sparsity-penalty|L1 penalty]] on those hidden activations. The penalty pushes activations to exactly zero rather than merely small. So on any given token, a hidden unit's output is either zero or it is not, with no threshold to argue about.

[[feature-density]] takes that at face value. Run the [[sparse-autoencoder]] over a stream of tokens. For each hidden unit, count the tokens on which its activation is nonzero, and divide by the number of tokens.

Nothing else enters. No person reads an example. No second model writes an explanation. It is a counter over forward passes the run is doing anyway.

That is the whole reason it survives as the working diagnostic. The other signals in [[evaluating-dictionary-learning]] that track what the paper wants — whether a hidden unit is a [[feature]] at all, whether it is [[monosemanticity|monosemantic]] — bottom out in [[manual-inspection]], which is slow and subjective. Density costs nothing and can be read after every run.

The axis choice follows from a hypothesis. The paper supposes the language model holds a large number of features spread across a wide distribution of densities, and that the rarer ones are harder for the autoencoder to find because they simply appear less often in its training data.

That supposition is also why the autoencoder was trained on 8 billion activation vectors from the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. The large dataset was an attempt to reach the rare end.

Densities of interest therefore run across orders of magnitude, from roughly one token in a hundred down to one in ten million. Plotted linearly they would all pile up against zero. So a run's densities go into a [[feature-density-histogram]] with a logarithmic horizontal axis, one bar per bucket, counting hidden units.

chapters.title: The three numbers, and what each is for
chapters.body:
The histogram is a picture, but the paper does not judge a run by its overall look. It reads three scalars off it.

The first is the number of live features sitting outside the [[ultralow-density-cluster]]. A dictionary of $N$ hidden units does not hand you $N$ features. Some units are dead. Some sit in the ultralow mode. What remains is the dictionary's working size — a yield, not a capacity.

The second is the lowest density at which a significant number of non-ultralow features still appear. This is the left edge of the working mode. Under the rarity hypothesis, that edge is how far down into rareness the run managed to reach. Pushing it further left means finding things that were previously invisible.

The third runs the other way. Count the features whose density is above 1%. A unit firing on more than one token in a hundred is firing thousands of times more often than the bulk of this run's interpretable features. The paper's reading is that a significant number of such features corresponds to an [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$ set too low. It states that as a correspondence it has observed, not as something derived.

So two numbers you want large or far left, one you want small. There is no combination rule and no threshold. The paper calls these, anecdotally, a decent proxy for subjective autoencoder performance and useful for quick iteration cycles.

It is also plain about the limit. It says it has identified some desiderata for the density distribution, but that much about the distribution remains not understood, and that this prevents density from giving a clear signal of progress.

The alternatives are worse or slower. [[training-loss-metric|Training loss]] cannot be compared across runs with different $\lambda$, because $\lambda$ changes the loss function. An [[information-based-metric]] was tried and failed to correlate with anything the authors cared about. [[l0-norm]] and [[loss-recovered-by-features]] do compare across runs, but cost a full evaluation pass.

chapters.title: Dead, alive, and the third thing
chapters.body:
The ideal the paper names is binary. A hidden unit either carries a real feature or is completely dead, and dead units are handled: [[dead-neurons]] are those with zero activation across a large number of datapoints, they waste dictionary capacity, and [[neuron-resampling]] periodically reinitializes them onto inputs the autoencoder currently reconstructs worst.

Now do the arithmetic on the left spike in [[fig-64]]. It sits around $10^{-7}$. Over 8 billion training tokens, that is on the order of eight hundred firings. A check asking whether a unit has fired at all in the last 12,500 training steps will find that it has.

So these units are never resampled. They are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]: dead in effect, alive by the test.

The case that they are a training artifact rather than something in the transformer rests on two observations. The first is the interpretability split. Anecdotally, almost every feature in the [[high-density-cluster]] is interpretable, and almost none in the ultralow mode are.

The second is stronger and is reported without numbers. Increase the number of training steps and the network kills off more ultralow units. A genuine property of the transformer should not be erased by running the autoencoder's optimizer for longer.

The paper hedges accordingly. The cluster *appears* to be an artifact; the source is still under investigation; the authors are still looking for ways either to mitigate these units or to detect and filter them automatically. As an aside, they suspect this density bimodality partly explains the bimodal [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]] that Huben reported between separately trained dictionaries — again, suspect.

Then [[external-replication]] cuts the other way. Trained on a different open-source one-layer model, more than half the features fell into an ultra-low cluster, though defined at below $10^{-4}$, two orders of magnitude looser than the paper's mode. Nearly all shared one encoder direction, but not one decoder direction. On a single input, 95% of them fired at once. The direction re-formed across random seeds, which the replicator reads as a fact about the model. Training an autoencoder constrained orthogonal to it produced a fresh ultra-low cluster in a new direction.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: When the two modes stop separating
chapters.body:
In many preliminary small-scale experiments the two clusters are perfectly separable — a visible gap you could put a line through. [[fig-65]] is where that stops. It is run A/5, with 131,072 hidden units, and the paper's stated condition for the failure is a large dictionary combined with a large sparsity penalty.

The humps sit on top of each other. The first of the three numbers — live features outside the ultralow mode — can no longer be read off, because there is no longer an outside to count.

This fails at exactly the wrong end. [[scaling-sparse-autoencoders|Scaling this method to larger models]] means larger dictionaries, so the diagnostic breaks where it will be needed most.

[[density-cluster-separation]] is the repair, and it is two extra coordinates per feature.

The first is that feature's bias: the single entry of the encoder bias vector belonging to that hidden unit, the scalar added before its ReLU. This is not the [[pre-encoder-bias]], which is one shared vector subtracted from every input before the encoder runs.

The second is the dot product between the feature's encoder vector and its decoder vector. The encoder row is the direction the unit projects onto in order to detect; the decoder column is the direction it writes back when it fires. This architecture does not tie them, so that dot product is free to take any value, and it carries information.

Plotted in those three dimensions, [[fig-66]] shows the high-density cluster coming apart cleanly again.

Two things to say plainly about the repair. The paper reports that these coordinates separate the clusters; it does not say why they do. And the diagnostic is no longer a glance at one histogram — it is a scatter in three dimensions with the boundary drawn by eye. Some of the cheapness that justified the measure has been spent.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: Wider dictionaries reach further down
chapters.body:
[[fig-67]] is the sweep. Five panels, one per sparsity setting. Within each panel, six density histograms overlaid, from dictionaries of 512 hidden units up to 131,072.

The bottom of that range is worth pausing on. 512 units is exactly the MLP's neuron count — a dictionary as wide as the layer and not [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]] at all, which under [[superposition]] is the one width guaranteed to be too narrow.

As width grows, two things could happen to the working mode. It could stay where it is and grow taller: more features, all of similar rarity. Or it could extend leftward: features rarer than anything the narrower runs held.

The paper reports the second. Widening finds not only more features but rarer ones. Its reading is that the features of this one-layer transformer have not been exhausted.

That inference is about a ceiling not yet hit, not a count of what is there. Nothing in the figure says where the left edge would eventually stop, and [[scaling-laws-for-dictionary-learning]] — the relations tying model size to the dictionary width and data needed — is named elsewhere as wanted and missing.

The reading also leans on the previous chapter. The ultralow mode grows with width too, so the newly reached rare units have to be separable from it; otherwise "rarer features" and "more of the third category" look the same. The largest of these six runs is the one where that separation failed.

Two qualifications on what the extra width buys. [[feature-splitting]] means some of it is not new territory but existing features dividing into narrower ones covering roughly the same ground. And [[autoencoder-width-limitation]] is the same claim seen from below: when the dictionary is narrower than the true feature set, the missing features do not vanish, they smear as weak activations across the ones that were learned.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.title: What the paper says it does not have
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.intro: The parent ran through these caveats in the paper's own order. Two different kinds are mixed together there: doubts about numbers already printed, which come with arithmetic behind them and with one line the discussion leaves in an appendix, and problems handed forward, which come with cost estimates. This level separates them and gives the reasoning under each.

chapters.title: The denominator, and where it came from
chapters.body:
The 79% is a ratio, and both halves of it are losses measured on the training data [[loss-recovered-by-features]].

The numerator: run the MLP activations through the autoencoder, put the reconstruction back into the forward pass in place of the real activations, and see how much the loss goes up.

The denominator: zero out the MLP layer entirely and see how much the loss goes up then [[zero-ablation-baseline]]. The substitution costs 21% of what deletion costs, so 79% of the layer's loss contribution is said to be recovered.

The appendix on hyperparameter selection adds a sentence the discussion section does not [[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat]]. A transformer with its MLP ablated may be an especially bad baseline, so the percentage is treated there as an overestimate.

The reason given is an ad hoc experiment, data not shown: similarly high percentages were reached by training a transformer from scratch with a small MLP. If a fraction of the layer's machinery gets most of the way, the denominator is easy to beat.

The long-tail worry has arithmetic under it too [[loss-recovery-caveats]]. A/1, the [[dictionary-learning-run]] the paper works in, has 4,096 features and recovers 79%. A/5 has 131,072 features and a lower [[l1-coefficient]] of 0.004, and recovers 94.5%.

That is thirty-two times the dictionary for the last fifteen points.

The question the authors say they would rather ask is what fraction of the model's [[true-features]] have been found. They cannot ask it. The count on the dictionary's side is a setting, since [[feature-splitting]] divides features further as the autoencoder widens, and the count on the model's side is unknown.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: The measure they cannot afford
chapters.body:
Section 4.2 opens by naming this the question the paper is least able to answer, and fraction-of-loss is only one way to pose it.

A better version is described [[explanation-based-loss-measure]]. Instead of splicing in the autoencoder's reconstruction, splice in activations predicted from each feature's written explanation. That would score the interpretation a human can read, rather than the reconstruction the autoencoder can produce — the two are not the same thing, and only the first is what the paper is claiming.

The machinery already exists in the [[automated-interpretability]] pipeline, where a language model predicts a feature's activation on a token from the explanation alone.

The cost is the problem. You would have to sample the explaining model once for every feature at every token. For a layer with 100,000 features, that is 100,000 times the cost of one sample from a model like Claude 2.

At the prices of the time, that put a single 4,096-token context at $12,500 to $25,000. One context is not an evaluation; many would be needed.

Approximations may exist, they say. A per-feature route is floated too: formalize feature importance as the independent loss contribution a feature makes, then ask how much of that particular contribution is recovered. They add that the conceptual issues there are significant.

The gap is wider than this one measure [[recognizing-good-features]]. [[manual-inspection]] remains the standard everything else stands in for, and it is slow. The hoped-for abstract alternative [[information-based-metric]] showed nothing on real data. And for comparing two dictionaries the paper wants measures beyond [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]], [[activation-similarity]] and [[attribution-similarity]].

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?
How much of the model does our interpretation explain?
Comparing features between two one-layer transformers
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

chapters.title: Where the activations actually are
chapters.body:
The interval scoring exists to defeat a specific failure of earlier evaluations [[max-dataset-example-bias]]. Judge a unit by its top-activating examples alone and a polysemantic neuron looks clean; the mixture only shows up further down.

So the annotator splits a feature's range into eleven bands evenly spaced from zero to its maximum activation [[activation-interval]], samples uniformly inside each, and scores each band against the hypothesis formed from the feature as a whole [[activation-interval-analysis]].

The result is not uniform. Many features stay consistent across the whole range. Others hold across roughly the top 60% and then fall off quickly as the activations shrink.

The paper offers one candidate cause and does not test it [[feature-at-slight-angle]]: a learned direction sitting at a small angle to the direction you actually wanted would behave inconsistently exactly at the weak end.

Now the mismatch. Those eleven bands are evenly spaced in activation, not in frequency, and most real firings are small [[low-interval-activation-skew]]. The bands that score worst are the bands a token is most likely to land in.

The defence re-weights the histogram by activation magnitude rather than counting tokens once each [[expected-value-plot]]. For the [[arabic-script-feature]], specificity to Arabic runs from 25% where the feature is barely on to 98% above an activation of 5, and almost all the activation mass sits in Arabic text.

Why magnitude should be the right weight is where the argument thins [[large-activations-dominate]]. Here it rests on [[linear-logit-effects]]. In larger models the paper says it follows from conjectures and heuristic arguments, holds for small activations by continuity, and has no watertight case.

The weak firings may also not be the feature's fault [[weak-activation-hypotheses]].

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron

chapters.title: Which features got looked at
chapters.body:
The manual experiment scored 412 activation intervals across 162 features and neurons, with the annotator not told which kind of unit was in front of him [[blinded-annotation]]. Those units were drawn uniformly from the run's dictionary [[manual-interpretability-scoring]].

Uniform over the dictionary is not uniform over use. A feature that fires on one token in a million counts the same as one that fires constantly.

That is the caveat [[interpretability-importance-caveat]]: interpretability might correlate with importance, in either direction. Two other samplings are named as things one could have done — the features with the largest activation magnitudes, or the ones with the largest effect when ablated [[feature-ablation]].

Neither was run. The authors say their sense, from having inspected the most active features, is that the important ones look better rather than worse. They also state the case they cannot rule out this way: the important features being systematically less interpretable.

What stands in for the experiment is an invitation. The published [[feature-exploration-interface]] covers every feature in every run, sorts by 'random' for an unbiased sample, and sorts by max activation and by [[feature-density]] — and readers are told to redo the test themselves.

The same selection pressure sits on the four detailed features, and the paper says so plainly [[cherry-picked-case-studies]]. They were chosen because a [[computational-proxy]] could be written for them — a cheap independent score for "is this Arabic script", "is this DNA".

For a feature about text concerning fantasy games, no such score exists. So the features carrying the strongest individual evidence are the ones a yardstick was easiest to build for.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?
Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

chapters.title: Twenty billion parameters, and what would remain
chapters.body:
Applying this to frontier models is called one of the most important questions going forward [[scaling-sparse-autoencoders]], and the paper prices it.

Take one MLP layer of a large model, width 10,000. A 100× [[expansion-factor]] gives a million dictionary directions. The encoder maps 10,000 dimensions to 1,000,000, which is $10^{10}$ weights; the decoder maps back, another $10^{10}$.

About 20 billion parameters. For one layer.

Then the data. Features here have densities running from roughly one token in a thousand down to one in a million, and rare features need to appear often enough to be learned at all — so the autoencoder may need a substantial fraction of the large model's own corpus. Training the reader could cost more than training what it reads.

The optimism is qualified. [[cunningham-et-al-parallel-work]] suggests the approach works on somewhat larger models, and the authors report preliminary results in the same direction without showing them. Their consolation is that the agenda then turns on an engineering and scaling problem, which frontier labs are good at.

What is missing is the shape of the curve [[scaling-laws-for-dictionary-learning]]. As the subject model grows, does the ideal expansion factor stay constant? How does the data requirement move? The question presumes there is a [[correct-number-of-features]] to aim at, and the paper notes that under some extensions of the hypothesis that may not be well posed.

Two problems sit outside all of this. Whether attention layers hold [[superposition]] too is untested [[attentional-superposition]]. And even a full solution leaves [[scalability-of-analysis]] — the [[curse-of-dimensionality-in-interpretability]] — where the only route named is delegating to AI, which they say may not fully satisfy.

n-the-unit-problem--the-counting-argumen.title: What Sparsity Has to Buy
n-the-unit-problem--the-counting-argumen.intro: The parent gave the shape of the problem: 4,096 unknowns, 512 measurements, sparsity as the tiebreaker. This level works out what that tiebreaker actually rests on — the geometry that makes a sparse solution unique, where the sparsity assumption was imported from, and how much weight the NP-hardness argument can really carry.

chapters.title: Inverting a very rectangular matrix
chapters.body:
Fix the dictionary. It is the decoder weight matrix $W_d$, 512 rows by 4,096 columns, whose columns are the directions of the learned [[feature]] set ([[dictionary-decoder]]). Ask for every $\mathbf{f}$ satisfying $W_d\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{x}$.

That is 512 linear equations in 4,096 unknowns. The solutions form an affine set: one particular solution plus anything in the null space of $W_d$. If the dictionary spans the 512-dimensional space, which a trained one will, that null space has dimension $4096 - 512 = 3584$.

So the answer is not slightly ambiguous. It is free along 3,584 independent directions.

Here is how sparsity cuts it down. Take two solutions, each with at most $k$ nonzero entries. Their difference has at most $2k$ nonzeros, and it lies in the null space. If no vector that sparse sits in the null space, the two solutions cannot differ. That is the standard [[compressed-sensing]] condition the paper is pointing at when it names the problem — and note where uniqueness comes from. It is a property of the dictionary's geometry, not of how many measurements you took.

The eight-to-one ratio is the [[expansion-factor]], and having more columns than rows is what the paper means by [[overcompleteness]]. Earlier [[dictionary-learning]] on transformer activations settled for an [[undercomplete-basis]] instead, fewer directions than dimensions, where the inversion is overdetermined and none of this arises.

One thing to carry forward. This paper never performs that recovery per datapoint. Its feature activations come out of [[eq-encoder]]: one linear map, one ReLU, weights frozen after training. No search, no iteration. The inversion is amortized into the encoder weights and then read off in a single forward pass.

chapters.title: Where the sparsity assumption actually comes from
chapters.body:
Trace the citation chain, because it is short and it never touches this transformer.

First, Olshausen and Field's "Why Sparseness?" — the [[sparsity-of-natural-latent-variables]] hypothesis. It is a claim about the variables generating natural data, made about natural images, long before language models.

Second, the paper's own prior work on SoLU models. The features anyone has looked at so far are, in the paper's word, "suggestive" of highly sparse variables. That is an impression from examples, not a distribution anyone measured.

Third, [[toy-models-of-superposition]] showed that a large set of sparse features *could* be packed as directions in a lower-dimensional space — the [[noisy-simulation]] picture behind [[superposition]]. A possibility result, on synthetic data with features sparse by construction.

None of the three measures how sparse the real features in this MLP layer are. [[feature-sparsity]] enters as a premise, and is then installed as an objective by the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]].

Which creates a closed loop worth stating plainly. The [[l0-norm]] reports how many features fire per token in the fitted decomposition. That is a property of the autoencoder that was trained to make it small. Assume sparsity, penalize for it, then measure it, and the measurement cannot confirm the assumption.

The paper does have one signal outside the loop, and builds on it deliberately. The fit sees MLP activations only ([[activations-only-decomposition]]); what a feature does to the logits is never an input. So coherent downstream effects are not something the objective could have manufactured — the paper's structural reply to the [[model-vs-data-question]]. It is evidence the decomposition found something the model uses. It is not evidence that the model's own features were sparse to begin with.

chapters.title: NP-hardness turned into a method argument
chapters.body:
Laid out flat, the argument runs in four steps.

Exact sparse recovery is NP-hard ([[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery]]). The transformer's own downstream components read these activations — in a one-layer model, the MLP down-projection and then the unembedding, two matrix multiplies. Whatever the model does with a feature, it gets there without solving anything NP-hard. So a [[dictionary-learning]] method strong enough for exact recovery could surface structure that has no reader inside the model.

Now test how much that carries. It is not a finding. Nobody ran Method of Optimal Directions or K-SVD here and showed them recovering unusable structure. The paper says "we have a concern that iterative dictionary learning methods might be *too strong*" — a worry about [[weak-dictionary-learning]], phrased as one.

And note the order in which the reasons are given. Scale comes first. The [[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms]] were tried and set aside, and the first reason offered is that a [[sparse-autoencoder]] scales to very large datasets. This autoencoder was trained on 8 billion datapoints, and the paper says scale mattered: more data made features subjectively "sharper" and more interpretable. Iterative solvers alternate a sparse-coding pass over the data with a dictionary update; that shape does not reach 8 billion.

Two reasons, then, and they are not equally solid. One is an engineering constraint the authors ran into. The other is an argument from what the model can compute, offered as a concern rather than a result.

The autoencoder route was not theirs alone — [[cunningham-et-al-parallel-work]] had been pushing on it in parallel, and the paper credits Sharkey et al. with focusing on it while this group was still exploring several approaches.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: Soft sparsity, and what it does not pin down
chapters.body:
The instrument that replaces the solver is calibrated by architecture. Bias in, linear layer and ReLU up, linear layer down — the same shape as the MLP layer being decomposed. The paper's claim is that it "should be similarly powerful in its ability to recover features from superposition." That is an analogy from architecture, not a bound on what either one can extract.

And the sparsity it enforces is soft. Nothing in [[sparse-autoencoder-loss]] forces an entry to zero; the L1 term makes zero cheap, ReLU makes it reachable, gradient descent does the rest. Compare [[topk-activation]], which keeps the $k$ largest activations and zeroes the rest by construction. The paper takes the soft route.

Soft sparsity has a leak. The penalty is on activation magnitudes, so shrinking an activation while lengthening its direction lowers the penalty and leaves the reconstruction untouched. That is why decoder columns are pinned to unit length ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]).

How sparse to make it has no principled answer here, and the paper says so: "we don't yet know of a principled way to determine a target level of sparsity." In practice they aim for an average $L^0$ below 10 or 20, distrust runs where it is a large fraction of 512, and pick the [[l1-coefficient]] off a frontier of sparsity against how much of the MLP's loss contribution survives reconstruction ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]], drawn in [[fig-68]]).

One thing the penalty buys quietly: because the dictionary is fit with MSE plus sparsity rather than cross-entropy, it has no incentive to pack features into its own units — the [[superposition-all-the-way-down]] worry.

And one thing it does not catch. A fixed-width dictionary with soft sparsity can smear a feature it lacks room for across many learned ones, as weak activations ([[autoencoder-width-limitation]]).

n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ab.title: Out to one-hot, and still polysemantic
n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ab.intro: The parent gave the argument as the paper gives it. This level asks how much weight it holds: what the sparse-architecture runs actually reported, which assumptions the four-feature calculation needs to work, how the numbers move when you loosen them, and what the verdict turns out to be a verdict about.

chapters.title: The experiments that got one clause
chapters.body:
The route had a target. [[activation-sparsity-training]] applies a constraint to the model being studied, during that model's own training, not to any analysis run afterwards. What is constrained is the count of nonzero MLP activations per token — the [[l0-norm|number of units on at once]], measured here on the transformer's own neurons rather than on any learned dictionary.

The reason to want it is the [[privileged-basis]]. The elementwise nonlinearity already singles the neuron basis out, so if features could also be forced to arrive one at a time, each neuron might end up carrying one thing. That would be [[monosemanticity]] built in rather than discovered.

The paper gives the program about four words of method. It says several attempts were made, "even to the point of training models with 1-hot activations". No architecture is named, no penalty, no dataset, no model size. A hard version would be a [[topk-activation]] with $k=1$, but the paper does not say that is what was run.

It also does not say what the constraint cost. With one nonzero coordinate the MLP writes a single decoder column, scaled, so the layer can only emit as many distinct directions as it has neurons. [[superposition]] is impossible after that, by counting. So is most of what the layer used to be able to do, and no loss number is reported.

The finding itself is one sentence in the contributions: models where neurons typically activated in isolation, and were still [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]]. Typically is not always, and no interpretability measure is named. Elsewhere the paper builds a blinded rubric and scores 412 activation intervals ([[manual-interpretability-scoring]]) precisely because it does not trust this judgement made casually.

Weight the paragraph accordingly. The runs are why these authors stopped. The counter-example is what they offer as why anyone else should.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

chapters.title: One bit, four outcomes
chapters.body:
Strip the setup down to what it is a model of.

The neuron fires or it does not. That is one bit. When it fires the model emits one fixed distribution over next tokens, and when it is silent it emits another. Nothing else varies. So the whole model is a map from one bit to two distributions, and the question [[cross-entropy-favors-polysemanticity|the calculation]] answers is how to spend that bit against four equally likely outcomes.

Start from knowing nothing. Guessing uniformly over four tokens costs $\ln 4 \approx 1.386$ nats on every token. Every strategy's job is to cut into that number.

The clean neuron cuts it to zero on a quarter of tokens and leaves $\ln 3 \approx 1.099$ on the other three quarters, averaging $0.824$. It has bought $1.386 - 0.824 = 0.562$ nats.

The ambiguous neuron halves the candidate set on every token instead: four down to two, whichever way the bit falls. That leaves $\ln 4 - \ln 2 = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ everywhere, so it has bought $0.693$ nats. That is exactly one bit, which is the most a single bit can buy.

So the point is not that vagueness is good. The point is that a balanced split of the outcomes extracts a full bit, and a one-against-three split does not, because three quarters of the time it announces only "not A", which rules out little.

Notice what is absent. There is one neuron, so there are no near-orthogonal directions and no [[interference]] anywhere in the arithmetic. The four [[feature|features]] being mutually exclusive is [[feature-sparsity]] pushed to its extreme. The argument in [[toy-models-of-superposition]] was about geometry; this one has no geometry in it at all. Prior work on [[polysemanticity-and-capacity]] treats the same preference in a general framework.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

chapters.title: Where the 0.13 nats goes
chapters.body:
The setup fixes five things at once: one binary neuron, four features, equal probabilities, mutual exclusivity, one correct token each. Two of them move the answer. The paper runs no variations, so what follows is arithmetic on its own setup.

Take frequency. Let A have probability $p$ and let B, C and D each have $q$, with $p + 3q = 1$. The clean neuron is silent on $3q$ of tokens and pays $\ln 3$ there, for $3q\ln 3$.

The ambiguous neuron should no longer predict a coin flip, because A and B are no longer equally likely; it predicts the conditional. Firing costs $p\ln\frac{p+q}{p} + q\ln\frac{p+q}{q}$, and the silent branch over C and D costs $2q\ln 2$.

Now set $p = 2q$. The firing branch becomes $2q\ln\frac{3}{2} + q\ln 3$, which is $3q\ln 3 - 2q\ln 2$. Add the silent branch and the $\ln 2$ terms cancel, leaving $3q\ln 3$ — the clean neuron's loss exactly.

The two tie when A is twice as likely as each rival, at $p = 0.4$. Above that the clean neuron wins. So $0.13$ nats is one point on a one-parameter family, and the family crosses zero close by. On the paper's own [[feature-density]] measure real features fire at rates spanning orders of magnitude, which makes equiprobability the least safe item on the list.

Count moves it the other way. With $n$ equally likely features the clean strategy pays $\frac{n-1}{n}\ln(n-1)$ against a balanced split's $\ln 2$. At $n=3$ they tie, at $n=4$ the gap is $0.13$, at $n=8$ it is about $0.32$.

Two assumptions go untouched. A ReLU neuron carries a magnitude rather than a bit, and a graded activation could in principle separate A from B. And four countable features is a strong idealisation, which the paper's own [[feature-splitting]] later strains — it ends up unsure whether there is a [[correct-number-of-features]] at all. Mutual exclusivity is the configuration it elsewhere calls [[mutually-exclusive-features-in-superposition|natural to pack together]], and the polysemantic neurons it documents mix things far less alike than A and B ([[classic-polysemantic-neuron-examples]]).

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron

chapters.title: From one neuron to a whole layer
chapters.body:
The paper spends one sentence on why a single-neuron toy says anything about a network. Push activation sparsity to its limit, only one neuron fires at a time, so take that neuron and the cases where it fires, and the same trade is on offer there.

Look at what the limit has done to the layer. If exactly one of $m$ neurons is nonzero per token, the MLP writes one decoder column, scaled. The layer is now a partition of input space into $m$ cells with one output direction per cell. It is a classifier with $m$ classes.

The toy calculation is then the local question inside a cell. Given that this neuron owns one, is the cell better drawn tightly around a single feature or loosely around several? The answer carries over for the reason it did before: a cell that fires rarely leaves most of the probability mass, and most of the entropy, in the silent branch where the model says nothing specific.

There is a second version the paper does not spell out. If the data has $n$ features and the layer has $m$ cells with $n \gg m$, every cell must cover several features whether the model prefers it or not. Ambiguity stops being a preference and becomes forced. That is a stronger conclusion, but it is a capacity argument, the same shape as [[noisy-simulation|the claim that a small layer is approximating a larger one]] — and $n \gg m$ is the ratio the paper later turns around and exploits, with an [[expansion-factor]] above one in its dictionary.

What is not covered is the middle. Nothing here treats a layer where two or ten neurons fire per token. The paper's own sentence is a belief and says so: models trained on cross-entropy will "generally prefer" polysemantic representations. A limit case and some unreported runs carry a claim about the whole regime.

This is [[polysemanticity-without-superposition]] at its widest. For [[mechanistic-interpretability]] the consequence is that neurons stay the wrong unit at every setting of the dial, which is where [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]] eventually lands.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

chapters.title: A verdict about the loss function
chapters.body:
The conclusion is usually repeated as a verdict on architecture. Read the sentence and it is a verdict on an objective.

Models trained on cross-entropy loss, the paper says, will generally prefer to represent more features polysemantically than to represent fewer [[true-features]] monosemantically. The subject of that sentence is the loss, not the design. And the next line says the obvious thing: models trained on other loss functions do not necessarily suffer this problem.

So [[architectural-approaches-to-superposition]] is not abandoned because architecture is powerless. It is abandoned because the quantity language models minimise pays for narrowing the distribution on every token, and ambiguity does exactly that. Under mean squared error the accounting differs: [[mse-loss-and-monosemanticity|polysemantic and monosemantic solutions can reach the same loss]], and the equal-loss minima found in [[engineering-monosemanticity|earlier toy work]] were minima of that kind.

Then comes the turn the rest of the paper depends on. The [[sparse-autoencoder-loss|objective the dictionary is trained under]] is mean squared error plus a sparsity penalty. The argument that closes the architectural route therefore does not reach the dictionary, where sparsity can inhibit superposition instead of being fought by the loss.

That is the paper's answer to [[superposition-all-the-way-down]], the worry that the learned features are themselves packed in superposition. It is an argument from the loss function, not a measurement. No test in the paper checks the dictionary for superposition directly.

Notice what the claim leaves open. It does not say how polysemantic a real language model's neurons are, does not size the preference at scale, and does not rule out interventions that reduce polysemanticity without removing it. What it rules out is fully monosemantic language models — an endpoint, not a gradient.

Of the [[three-approaches-to-superposition]] laid out earlier, the first is now closed. [[dictionary-learning]] after the fact is the one the paper takes, and part of why it can is that MSE is a loss it gets to choose.

n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ho.title: One Matrix Multiply Per Token
n-why-decomposition-and-not-redesign--ho.intro: The parent gave the encoder's equation and the argument for keeping it weak. This level writes out the actual sizes and constraints, unpacks what a single-shot linear readout gives up against a per-datapoint search, and walks the toy loss calculation that the "not superposition again" argument rests on — separating, at each step, what the paper measured from what it asserts.

chapters.title: What each term is doing
chapters.body:
Sizes first. The transformer being decomposed has a 128-dimensional residual stream and a 512-neuron ReLU MLP [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. What the dictionary is fitted to is that MLP's 512 post-ReLU activations at a single token position [[mlp-activations-as-target]], as [[fig-2]] lays out.

The dictionary used through most of the paper has 4,096 hidden units. The encoder's own matrix [[autoencoder-encoder]] is therefore $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{4096 \times 512}$, the decoder matrix is $W_d \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 4096}$, and the biases $\mathbf{b}_e$ and $\mathbf{b}_d$ have length 4,096 and 512. More dictionary directions than the space has dimensions is the [[overcompleteness]] the whole setup rests on.

Three of those four tensors are unconstrained. The fourth is not: the columns of $W_d$ are held at unit norm. Each column is one [[feature-direction]], the vector a feature writes along when it fires, and normalizing the columns keeps the magnitude in the activation rather than in the direction. The paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" for this same matrix [[dictionary-decoder]].

The bias in front of the encoder is not an extra parameter. The same vector is subtracted from the input before the encoder and added back after the decoder, deliberately tied [[pre-encoder-bias]]. It is initialized to the geometric median of the activation dataset. The effect is that everything is measured from the middle of the activation cloud instead of from the origin, so the threshold deciding whether a [[feature-activation]] is zero at all sits somewhere sensible. The paper puts this first in its ordered list of modifications, on the strength of toy-model experiments.

The training objective is reconstruction plus sparsity [[sparse-autoencoder-loss]]. One asymmetry in it is easy to read past. The reconstruction term is a mean over the 512 vector elements; the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] is a sum over all 4,096 hidden values. The two terms are not on a common footing, and what a given coefficient means depends on both conventions [[sparse-autoencoder]].

chapters.title: Shaped like the layer it reads
chapters.body:
The claim being made is a comparison, so put the two stacks side by side. The MLP the encoder is reading applies a matrix to the residual stream, adds a bias, and clips at zero. The encoder applies a matrix to a recentred activation vector, adds a bias, and clips at zero. Three operations each, in the same order.

Why the paper wants that resemblance rather than something better. Recovering a sparse high-dimensional vector from a low-dimensional projection is [[compressed-sensing]], and in its exact form it is NP-hard. The transformer is plainly not running an NP-hard search on every token. If the decomposition were produced by a method that could, the coefficients it reports would be facts about the geometry of the activations rather than about anything the model can read out of them, which is the whole of [[weak-dictionary-learning]] as a worry.

The link to [[superposition]] is what makes this more than pedantry. Superposition is only workable because of [[feature-sparsity]]: few features are active on any one token, which is also the assumption that makes [[dictionary-learning]] tractable at all. Feature directions packed more densely than the dimension allows cannot all be orthogonal, so any linear readout of one direction collects some of whatever else is currently active, which is [[interference]]. Pulling features back out of superposition means beating that interference. The paper's position is that whatever the MLP layer can beat, an encoder of the same shape should be able to beat too.

Two things the resemblance argument does not establish. It is a resemblance, not a proof of equal recovery power, and no bound is offered. And the shapes are not identical: the MLP expands 128 dimensions to 512, a factor of four, while the encoder expands 512 to 4,096, a factor of eight. The encoder also reads a [[privileged-basis]] — the MLP's neuron coordinates, singled out by the elementwise ReLU — that the layer producing them did not read.

Comparing features between two one-layer transformers
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: The search, moved into the weights
chapters.body:
A classical solver works one datapoint at a time. It commits to a coefficient, subtracts that direction's contribution from the input, and looks again at what is left, so a large coefficient can suppress a rival that would otherwise have fired on the same evidence. The encoder cannot do any of that [[amortized-sparse-coding-approximation]]. There is no residual to re-examine and no second pass, so a feature's response to an input is a fixed linear function of that input, whatever else is firing.

The compensation is that the encoder matrix was fitted, once, against the statistics of the whole activation distribution. The cost moves from inference into training, and the training bill is large: roughly 10 billion activation vectors were harvested from 40 million Pile contexts, and just over 8 billion of them used [[autoencoder-training-dataset]].

Fitting one fixed map well turned out to need extra machinery. Hidden units go dead, meaning they stop firing across large numbers of datapoints, and are periodically reinitialized to point at datapoints the autoencoder currently reconstructs worst [[neuron-resampling]]. Learning rate was swept alongside training length, with lower rates and more steps reported to yield more real features [[learning-rate-sweep]]. Renormalizing the dictionary columns after every step interacts badly with Adam's moment estimates, and the paper describes a correction for it [[adam-decoder-normalization-interaction]].

Dead units are worth dwelling on, because they are amortization's characteristic failure. A row of the encoder matrix that never wins any input is a wasted slot, and the paper's quickest diagnostic, [[feature-density]], is essentially a way of counting how many slots are doing work.

The evidence here is labelled as what it is. The paper offers these choices as intuition and anecdotal evidence rather than clean ablations, because they arrived at different points in the research and interact with each other.

Interaction Between Adam and Decoder Normalization

chapters.title: Tilted away from the transpose
chapters.body:
Tying the encoder to the decoder would make the encoder matrix the transpose of the dictionary, and the consequence is concrete. A feature's pre-activation would then be the inner product of the recentred input with that feature's own dictionary vector, plus a bias. Now take two features whose dictionary vectors have cosine similarity near one. When the first fires at some strength, the second's pre-activation picks up almost all of that strength for free, and only the bias stands between it and firing too.

Untying lets each encoder row rotate away from its own dictionary vector, toward whatever direction best separates that feature from its neighbours [[untied-decoder-weights]]. The paper reports exactly this in its trained models: features with closely related dictionary vectors end up with encoder vectors that are still similar but tilted further apart, which it reads as preventing confusion between them [[encoder-decoder-offset-crosstalk]].

Its worked case is the base64 group [[base64-feature-family]]. In the 512-feature dictionary there is a single base64 feature, A/0/45, firing across whole base64 strings. In the 4,096-feature dictionary it appears as three [[fig-48]]. A/1/2357 fires preferentially on letters [[base64-feature]], A/1/2364 on digits, and A/1/1544 on base64 that decodes to readable ASCII [[fig-50]]. This is the paper's [[feature-splitting]] story arriving from the other side, as several features covering one apparent concept rather than one feature covering many [[multiple-features-for-one-context]].

How strong is the evidence. The tilt is reported qualitatively, as vectors being "more tilted away", with no cosine similarities given for either the dictionary vectors or the encoder vectors, and no tied-weight control run to compare against. What is offered is a mechanism and one example consistent with it.

chapters.title: Why the dictionary is argued not to do it too
chapters.body:
The remaining worry is recursive. If the model packs features into directions more densely than it has coordinates, why would the dictionary not do the same thing inside itself, giving superposition all the way down [[superposition-all-the-way-down]]?

The paper's answer runs through the loss function, and it reuses the argument that closed off the architectural route [[architectural-approaches-to-superposition]]. Train a model to have sparse activations and superposition does go away, but the neurons stay polysemantic [[polysemanticity-without-superposition]]. The toy calculation is worth walking. Take one binary neuron and four mutually exclusive features A/B/C/D, each predicting its own token. Let the neuron fire only on A and predict A correctly, leaving a uniform guess over B/C/D the rest of the time: the cross-entropy is three quarters of $\ln 3$, about 0.8. Now let it fire on both A and B, predicting uniformly over those two, and predict uniformly over C and D when it is silent: that is $\ln 2$, about 0.7. The ambiguous neuron wins. Cross-entropy training therefore prefers [[polysemanticity]] to [[monosemanticity]] on its own terms, with or without superposition.

The decomposition is not trained on cross-entropy. It is trained on squared error plus a sparsity penalty, and under squared error the paper cites results where polysemantic and monosemantic solutions score equally, and where for some importance curves the monosemantic one is actively preferred. That is the argument in full: sparsity can inhibit superposition from forming in the learned dictionary, because this loss does not reward ambiguity the way the model's own loss does.

Note where that leaves it. The claim is an inference from the objective, resting on [[toy-models-of-superposition]] and two citations, and the paper makes it in a parenthetical aside. No check on the trained dictionary's own hidden units is reported. [[three-approaches-to-superposition]] places this branch among the alternatives.

n-the-model-and-the-tool--the-objective-.title: A tool chosen for what it cannot do
n-the-model-and-the-tool--the-objective-.intro: The parent named the inner problem and the two reasons for sidestepping it. This level puts numbers on all four steps: how underdetermined the problem actually is, what "NP-hard in its exact form" refers to, what the classical methods run per datapoint and what that would cost here, and how much weight the weakness argument can carry.

chapters.title: 512 equations, 4,096 unknowns
chapters.body:
Fix the sizes first, because the whole argument runs on them.

At one token position, the thing being decomposed is the post-ReLU activation vector of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]'s MLP: 512 numbers. The dictionary the paper focuses on, run A/1, has 4,096 columns. Its widest run has 131,072.

Now write down what solving for the codes means. The [[linear-feature-decomposition]] says $\mathbf{x} \approx \mathbf{b} + \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{d}_i$, where each [[feature-direction]] $\mathbf{d}_i$ is a fixed unit vector and each [[feature-activation]] $f_i$ is a scalar to be found. With the directions held fixed, that is 512 equations in 4,096 unknowns.

Subtract. 4,096 minus 512 leaves 3,584 directions along which the code vector can be moved without changing the reconstruction at all — the null space of the dictionary matrix.

So the "answer" is not a vector. It is a 3,584-dimensional family of vectors, every one of which reproduces $\mathbf{x}$ exactly.

Sparsity is the condition that picks one out of that family: take the point with the fewest nonzero entries. That is [[compressed-sensing]].

The paper does not treat sparsity as a solver's convenience. It is the same assumption that motivated the setup. Natural latent variables are argued to be sparse; the features already glimpsed in language models look [[feature-sparsity|highly sparse]]; and [[toy-models-of-superposition]] showed that many sparse features can be packed as directions into a smaller space, at the cost of [[interference]] between them.

Note where the difficulty comes from. It exists only because the dictionary has more columns than the space has dimensions. [[overcompleteness]] is exactly what the paper says separates its setting from work seeking as many factors as dimensions — with a square dictionary you would simply invert and be done.

And note what is deliberately unused: the codes are computed from $\mathbf{x}$ alone, with no reference to what $\mathbf{d}_i$ does to later layers. That is what lets [[dictionary-learning]] here hold downstream effects back as an independent check.

chapters.title: What exactly is NP-hard, and what the classics do instead
chapters.body:
"NP-hard in its exact form" names a specific problem: minimise the number of nonzero entries in $\mathbf{f}$ — the [[l0-norm]] — subject to reconstructing $\mathbf{x}$.

That objective is combinatorial rather than continuous. A count of nonzeros gives gradient descent nothing to descend; it is flat everywhere and jumps at zero. What you are really doing is choosing a subset of dictionary columns to switch on, then least-squares fitting inside it.

Walk the size of that choice. The paper targets fewer than 10 or 20 active features per token. Choosing 10 columns out of 4,096 gives roughly $4096^{10}/10!$ subsets, on the order of $10^{30}$ — per activation vector. That is [[np-hardness-of-exact-sparse-recovery]] in concrete terms.

[[classical-dictionary-learning-algorithms]] do not solve that problem. They take one of two escapes, and the paper names both. Relax it: replace the count of nonzeros with the sum of magnitudes, an [[l1-sparsity-penalty]], which is convex and can be minimised. Or search greedily: repeatedly take the column most aligned with whatever is still unexplained, subtract its contribution, and go again.

The relaxed form is the one the paper ends up keeping anyway, as the penalty term in the [[sparse-autoencoder-loss]].

Method of Optimal Directions and K-SVD then wrap one of those inner solvers in an outer alternation: solve for all the codes with the dictionary fixed, update the dictionary with the codes fixed, repeat.

The shape to notice is the nesting. An iterative solve sits inside the loop — once per datapoint, at every dictionary update, and again every time you want the code for a new activation.

The paper's own gloss is that recovery being possible at all is "kind of miraculous". Storing sparse high-dimensional structure in a smaller space is the easy half. Getting it back out is the hard one.

One thing the paper does not supply: it says several classic methods were tried, but not which, not what they produced, and not how they compared. Its later checks on whether the decomposition works ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]) are all applied to the method it kept.

chapters.title: Moving the search into the weights
chapters.body:
Set the encoder beside that nesting.

$$f_i(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_e(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d) + \mathbf{b}_e\big)_i$$

One matrix multiply, one bias, one threshold. No residual to recompute, no column to pick, nothing revisited. Whatever answer the [[sparse-autoencoder]] gives for an activation vector, it gives on the first pass.

The search has not been skipped. It has been moved. Gradient descent spends the whole of training looking for a single $W_e$ whose one-shot answer is good on average across the activation distribution, and that one $W_e$ is then reused for every vector afterwards. This is [[amortized-sparse-coding-approximation]] — an inner loop replaced by a fixed function, fitted once.

The once is large. The [[autoencoder-training-dataset]] is built by running the transformer over 40 million Pile contexts and collecting the post-ReLU MLP vector at each token, which yields around 10 billion of them.

Training runs 1 million steps at a batch size of 8,192. Multiply those and you get about 8.2 billion, which is why just over 8 billion of the pool gets used. Sampling is [[sampling-without-replacement|without replacement]], so essentially no vector is seen twice, and the paper says not repeating data matters for results. Vectors are subsampled at 250 tokens per context and shuffled, so one batch spans many contexts rather than a handful ([[activation-shuffling]]).

Set that number against the previous chapter. Eight billion inner solves, each a relaxation or a greedy search, is a different order of expense from eight billion matrix multiplies.

The evidence for the scale argument is soft. The authors report that training on more data made features subjectively "sharper" and more interpretable — a judgement about how the features read, not a measurement. The published sweeps ([[fig-68]]) vary dictionary size and sparsity, not dataset size.

The approach is not this paper's invention. It credits a [[cunningham-et-al-parallel-work|parallel line of interim reports]] for committing to the sparse autoencoder while this group was still trying several things at once, with [[prior-dictionary-learning-on-embeddings|older sparse coding work on word embeddings]] behind both.
