chapters.title: The argument for wanting a weak tool
chapters.body:
The second reason is not about cost. It is about not wanting the tool to work too well.

Suppose some iterative method did recover $\mathbf{f}$ accurately. Nothing about that guarantees the transformer can. Whatever reads the MLP output downstream does so through linear maps and elementwise nonlinearities, and the model plainly does not run an NP-hard search anywhere in its forward pass.

So a decomposition could be extractable from the activations while being unavailable to the network that produced them.

Why that would matter: the aim is to describe the model's computation. Structure present in the activations but unreadable by the model is closer to a fact about the data distribution than about the layer — the [[model-vs-data-question]] the paper takes up separately using downstream effects.

The reply is architectural. An encoder that is a linear map followed by a ReLU is, in shape, an MLP layer. If anything downstream pulls features out of [[superposition]], that is the operation doing it, so the autoencoder should be about as able to do it as the model is. That is [[weak-dictionary-learning]].

Weigh it honestly. It is an analogy between architectures, not a bound. No number is offered comparing what $W_e$ recovers against what any downstream circuit actually reads, and none could be read off the paper's evaluations.

The paper's own results suggest reach is a matter of degree rather than a matched pair. Widening the dictionary keeps splitting features into finer ones rather than exhausting them ([[feature-splitting]], visible across the density histograms in [[fig-67]]), and no run recovers all of the layer's behaviour ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]).

Being too weak has its own failure mode. The features the paper cares most about are the ones [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis|with no counterpart among the neurons]] — spread across many coordinates, which is what a single readout direction has to work to find, and what makes [[polysemanticity]] hard to see through in the first place.

One nearby worry the paper does answer: whether the dictionary might itself put features in superposition ([[superposition-all-the-way-down]]).

n-the-model-and-the-tool--modifications-.title: Seeding the dead on the worst-fit inputs
n-the-model-and-the-tool--modifications-.intro: This level walks the procedure in the order it runs, and sets each number against the ones around it: where the four resampling events sit inside a million-step run, what the sampling weight comes to when the quantity being squared is already a square, and which parts of the recipe the paper leaves unstated.

chapters.title: Four appointments in the first tenth
chapters.body:
The four checks are scheduled at training steps 25,000, 50,000, 75,000 and 100,000. Set that against the length of the run. The autoencoder is trained for one million update steps, well past the point where the loss curve looks flat ([[extended-training-steps]]).

So every resampling event happens inside the first tenth of training. Nothing is revived after step 100,000. A unit that goes quiet at step 300,000 stays quiet for the remaining seven hundred thousand steps.

The other side of the same arithmetic is more encouraging. A unit revived at the last appointment still has 900,000 steps ahead of it. [[neuron-resampling]] is an early-training intervention, not a maintenance loop that runs throughout.

The look-back window is 12,500 steps, which is half the gap between appointments. The check at 50,000 therefore inspects only the second half of the interval since the previous one, and a unit is judged on that window alone ([[dead-neurons]]).

Now the pool's size in context. Each step draws a batch of 8,192 activation vectors, and vectors are drawn [[sampling-without-replacement|without replacement]] across the whole run, so a million steps consume $10^6 \times 8192 = 8.192$ billion of the roughly ten billion vectors collected ([[autoencoder-training-dataset]]).

Divide 8,192,000,000 by 819,200 and you get exactly 10,000. The seed pool is one ten-thousandth of the data the autoencoder ever sees.

Small, but not narrow. Activations are subsampled at 250 tokens per context and shuffled before batching ([[activation-shuffling]]), so a random pool of that size still spans an enormous number of separate documents.

chapters.title: Squaring a number already squared
chapters.body:
The objective is $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|X|}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in X} \|\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{f}\|_1$ ([[sparse-autoencoder-loss]]).

Take the first term on its own ([[mse-reconstruction-term]]). It is already the squared distance between an activation and its reconstruction. [[loss-proportional-input-sampling|The draw]] then squares that.

So the sampling weight goes as the fourth power of the distance. In those terms: an input whose reconstruction misses by twice the Euclidean distance of another is $2^4 = 16$ times as likely to be picked. At three times the distance it is 81 times as likely.

Now the ambiguity. The paper writes "the autoencoder's loss on that input", and the loss as defined has two terms.

The second is the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]], weighted by [[l1-coefficient|the coefficient $\lambda$]]. Note the asymmetry in how the two are computed: the reconstruction term is a mean over the vector's elements, while the L1 is a sum over the [[feature-activation|feature activations]]. Their relative size depends on $\lambda$ and on how many features happen to fire.

If the sparsity term is included, the draw is pulled toward inputs the autoencoder represents expensively as well as toward ones it represents badly. Those are not the same set. An input with a high [[l0-norm|$L^0$]] can still be reconstructed accurately.

The paper states the design intent as seeding features to fit "inputs where the current autoencoder performs worst", which reads toward reconstruction error. It does not say which, and reports no comparison between the two readings.

chapters.title: A datapoint pressed into service
chapters.body:
What gets copied into the dictionary is an actual MLP activation vector, collected after the transformer's ReLU. Every one of its coordinates is therefore non-negative.

The new column of $W_d$ ([[dictionary-decoder]]) starts life inside the positive orthant. A random draw would not.

The renormalization throws the vector's length away ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]). Only the direction is kept, and how much of it the reconstruction uses is left for the unit's activation to decide.

One detail the recipe leaves open. The autoencoder subtracts a learned [[pre-encoder-bias]] from every input before encoding, and the paper says to renormalize "the input vector" without saying whether that means $\mathbf{x}$ or $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$. The two differ by a fixed vector, initialized to the geometric median of the activation dataset, so the resulting directions differ too.

Then the more substantial limit on what a seed can be.

A single activation vector is not one feature's contribution. Under [[superposition]] it is a sum of the [[feature-direction|directions]] of every [[feature]] active on that token, each scaled by how strongly that feature fired.

So the seeded column is a mixture. It is a guess at where unexplained structure lives, not a [[true-features|true feature]] recovered.

And the mixing is likely to be worst exactly here. The input was chosen because it is badly reconstructed, which often means several unrepresented features overlap on it. The seed then points along their sum rather than along any one of them.

Gradient descent still has to do the separating. What resampling supplies is a starting point inside the region of activation space the current dictionary fails to cover ([[dictionary-learning]]). A random column is unlikely to land there at all.

Interaction Between Adam and Decoder Normalization

chapters.title: Born aligned, then allowed to tilt
chapters.body:
The scale factor is not an absolute constant. The revived unit's encoder row is set to $0.2$ times the average encoder norm of the units still alive ([[resampled-encoder-scaling]]), so the rule is stated relative to the network's current state.

Encoder norms drift over a million steps. The rule drifts with them. A unit revived at step 100,000 is therefore quiet by the same relative margin as one revived at 25,000.

Now the direction it is given. Encoder and decoder are learned independently here ([[untied-decoder-weights]]), and the paper reports that trained encoder rows are not the transpose of their decoder columns.

The reason it offers is specific. Features with closely related dictionary vectors end up with encoder rows tilted away from them, which stops each from firing on the other's inputs ([[encoder-decoder-offset-crosstalk]]). The [[autoencoder-encoder|encoder]] is doing a job the decoder is not — a single linear pass standing in for an iterative sparse coding procedure ([[amortized-sparse-coding-approximation]]).

Resampling hands the revived unit the tied configuration, encoder parallel to decoder. That is the arrangement trained units move away from. The tilt has to be learned back.

Then the optimizer state ([[adam-state-reset-on-resampling]]).

On the decoder side there is a further reason it could not be carried over. Because dictionary columns are held at unit norm, the paper does not renormalize after each step; it removes the gradient component parallel to the column before stepping ([[adam-decoder-normalization-interaction]]).

Adam's moments for that column are accumulated in the tangent space of one particular direction. Resampling replaces the direction. The stored moments describe a geometry that is gone.

Interaction Between Adam and Decoder Normalization

chapters.title: What the comparison shows, and what it doesn't
chapters.body:
The claimed gains are stated in the paper's proxies, not in interpretability directly. Resampling yields more features in the [[high-density-cluster]] of the [[feature-density-histogram]], and a lower total loss ([[training-loss-metric]]).

Both are stand-ins. The paper says plainly that measuring interpretability is difficult and slow, so changes get tested against proxies like these ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]).

No numbers accompany the comparison. The two baselines are named — no resampling, and reinitializing the same weights with [[kaiming-uniform-initialization]] — and the outcome is given as "outperforms", with no table, no curve and no count.

The paper gives its reason. Its modifications appeared at different points in the research and interact with each other, so it supplies intuition and anecdotal evidence in place of rigorous ablations.

There is also a complication inside the metric being improved. Training longer kills off more units in the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], and those units fire so rarely they were barely contributing anyway ([[de-facto-dead-neurons]]). A count of dead units understates how much of the dictionary is inert, which is part of why the paper reads the density clusters rather than the dead count ([[feature-density-diagnostics]]).

The costs are admitted directly. Loss still spikes, and resampling too frequently makes training diverge.

Deadness also has causes the paper lists separately: learning rate too high, batch size too low, redundant data, too many steps, choice of optimizer. Some of those are addressed on their own terms ([[learning-rate-sweep]]).

That leaves resampling as one treatment among several, applied to a symptom whose sources are partly known. The [[lottery-ticket-hypothesis]] is offered as something the procedure "may be compatible with", and no test of it is proposed. The authors call better resampling strategies an open area of their own research.

n-does-the-feature-do-anything--dna-base.title: What a correlation of 0.38 is measuring
n-does-the-feature-do-anything--dna-base.intro: Above, the two mechanisms behind the 0.38 were named. Here the proxy is built up from its formula, so each mechanism can be priced against it — and then the question turns around: with both false positives set aside, what is the number still counting?

chapters.title: The score, character by character
chapters.body:
The [[base64-proxy]] is one instance of a general form. Every proxy in the paper is a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: how much more likely a string looks under the feature's hypothesis than under the data at large. Written out, $\log\big(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s)\big)$.

The numerator is the [[character-distribution-proxy]]. Take natural logs and each legal character contributes $\ln(1/64) \approx -4.16$. A clean twenty-character run therefore scores about $-83$ up top.

Each illegal character contributes $\ln(10^{-10}) \approx -23.0$ instead. One space costs roughly nineteen more than a legal character would. That is the veto, priced.

The denominator is estimated on a different basis. $P(s)$ comes from a [[unigram-p-s-estimate]]: a product of independent unigram probabilities, one factor per *token*.

So the two halves of the ratio are counted in different units — characters above, tokens below. Ordinary English packs many characters into few tokens, each reasonably common. A base64 run of the same length breaks into more tokens, each rare. The denominator falls away faster than the numerator does, and the ratio climbs.

One further piece matters for what follows. A feature's activation at a token can depend on what preceded it, so the [[computational-proxy]] is not evaluated on a single fixed window. It is computed over several prefixes ending at the token in question, and the maximum is taken ([[prefix-maximization]]).

An illegal character earlier in the line therefore does not spoil the score. The maximization simply finds a later, cleaner window.

The proxy is thus eager by construction. Any run of legal characters long enough to be unusual under the unigram model will score high, whatever else that run happens to be. Where a proxy's distribution is sharply bimodal, the paper reduces the score to its sign ([[proxy-binarization]]) before using it to colour a histogram of [[base64-feature]] activations.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

chapters.title: Hexadecimal scores exactly as well
chapters.body:
Now feed that formula an uppercase hexadecimal string. Its alphabet is `[0-9A-F]` — sixteen characters.

Check them against `[a-zA-Z0-9+/]`. The ten digits are in. `A` through `F` are in. Every character of every hexadecimal string is base64-legal.

So the numerator takes no penalty at all. A twenty-character hex run scores the same $-83$ that a genuine base64 run of that length scores. Not approximately the same — identically, because the model gives every legal character the same $1/64$ and does not care which one it is.

The denominator behaves as before. Hex fragments are rare tokens under the unigram model, so $P(s)$ is small and the ratio comes out large. The proxy is as confident that hexadecimal is base64 as it is about base64 itself.

Nothing in the formula could have caught this. A real base64 string draws on lowercase letters, on `+`, on `/`; a hex string never does. Across a long run that absence is strong evidence — but the proxy scores each character independently against a flat distribution, and has no term for what a run as a whole fails to contain.

The model does draw the distinction. [[hexadecimal-feature]] A/1/3817 is a feature of its own for exactly that context. Nor is it a one-off: the paper reports a hexadecimal feature in the smaller 512-feature dictionary as well, and had already found a hexadecimal neuron next to the base64 neuron in an earlier SoLU model ([[solu-base64-neuron]]). It is one of the paper's [[context-features]], staying on across a whole region of text of a given kind.

On hexadecimal, then, the proxy reads high and A/1/2357 reads zero. Each such token is a large residual in the [[pearson-correlation]] behind [[feature-proxy-correlation]]. The residual belongs to the yardstick, and sits in the paper's catalogue of [[proxy-limitations]].

chapters.title: The merge that never happens
chapters.body:
[[byte-pair-encoding]] builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in the corpus. Digit pairs are frequent in ordinary text, so a pair like `89` earns its own token early.

That merge is then applied everywhere, including inside base64 strings, where the digits carry no numeric meaning at all.

Follow the consequence. Suppose a base64 string contains `...Bq89mp...`. The tokenizer produces `[Bq][89][mp]`. The sequence `[Bq][8][9][mp]` cannot occur — there is no input the tokenizer would encode that way.

Turn that around. If the current token is a single digit standing alone, the character after it is not a digit. Had it been, the two would have merged.

That is usable information. Under the uniform character model the next character is a digit with probability $10/64$. Conditioned on the current token being a lone digit, it is close to zero.

The model uses it. [[base64-digit-feature]] A/1/2364 fires on digits in base64 contexts, and [[fig-49]] shows what it does downstream: its logit weights track A/1/2357's closely across the vocabulary, except that the ten digit tokens are pushed far lower. The same prediction about base64, minus the digits.

Why A/1/2357 leaves that territory alone is [[feature-splitting]]. In the 512-feature run a single feature, A/0/45, covered whole base64 strings. At 4,096 features it divides into three ([[fig-48]]): letters, digits, and base64 that decodes to readable ASCII ([[fig-50]]). Together they form the [[base64-feature-family]], an instance of [[multiple-features-for-one-context]].

The proxy sees none of it. Its numerator runs over characters, where a digit is worth $1/64$ like anything else. Tokens never enter the formula, so the merge it would have to notice is invisible to it. The feature is tracking the tokenizer rather than the content — what the paper calls [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]].

chapters.title: What fig-25 can and cannot settle
chapters.body:
[[fig-25]] is an [[activation-spectrum-by-proxy]]. Every token in a sample is placed in a bar by how hard A/1/2357 fired on it, and each bar is split by the proxy's verdict. Read upward, the strong bars are almost entirely proxy-positive.

That is a claim about [[activation-specificity]]: given the feature is on, the context is base64.

The 0.38 is a different claim. It is a correlation taken over all sampled tokens, so it also charges the feature for every token where the proxy is high and the feature is off. That is [[activation-sensitivity]] — the half the paper repeatedly finds weaker, and routinely patched by sibling features.

Both mechanisms land in the correlation, but they are not the same kind of case. Hexadecimal is proxy error with no base64 present anywhere. Digits are real base64 where a sibling has the job.

The correlation cannot tell those apart. Neither can fig-25: all of those tokens sit in one enormous bar at zero activation, which no colouring can resolve.

Note what is not done here. The paper gives no figure for how much of the shortfall hexadecimal accounts for, and no correlation recomputed with hex excluded. For the [[dna-feature]] it built a disagreement grid, [[fig-21]], sampling the cases where feature and [[dna-proxy]] disagree and auditing them one by one. No equivalent grid appears for base64.

So the account is a decomposition offered by example, not a measured one. The paper's own wording keeps the hedge — the 0.38 is "mostly" the proxy being too broad. Its general list of reasons a feature can look impure at low activations ([[weak-activation-hypotheses]]) is not ruled out for this feature, and no [[expected-value-plot]] is shown here to weigh the weak bars by how much they actually move the logits.

chapters.title: Why the logit picture shades instead of splitting
chapters.body:
A [[logit-weight]] is one number per vocabulary token, saying how much that token's next-token logit moves when the feature fires. In this one-layer model the path from feature to output is close to linear ([[linear-logit-effects]]), so the number is a fair summary of what the feature does.

Softmax is shift-invariant, so these weights have no absolute zero. The paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]).

The recurring shape is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]]: a tall mode near zero covering most of the vocabulary, plus a small mode far to the right holding tokens specific to the feature's context.

For the feature matched to the [[arabic-script-proxy]], those two modes come apart cleanly. A token is in Arabic script or it is not, with little in between. [[fig-26]] does not come apart cleanly.

The paper's reason concerns the vocabulary rather than the feature. `fr` is a plausible base64 token and also a common abbreviation for French. Any token built from English letters can turn up inside a base64 string with nontrivial probability.

So "base64 token" is a matter of degree, and caution is warranted: pushing `fr` hard costs whenever the context is actually French, and `fr` already carries a prior from that other use.

This costs something when reading the picture. The central mode is what the paper calls [[weight-interference]] — crosstalk it attributes to [[superposition]], where feature directions cannot all be orthogonal, so activating one slightly activates others ([[interference]]). For base64 that mode overlaps the base64 tokens rather than sitting apart from them, and the paper expects the overlap to come from base64 tokens being used elsewhere.

Which leaves the two readings tangled. A token near zero might be there by interference, or because the model deliberately gives it only a small push. Nothing in the [[logit-weight-histogram]] separates them for this feature. The interference reading is not contradicted here; it is simply not tested.

n-from-four-features-to-the-population--.title: What the Three Probes Actually Compute
n-from-four-features-to-the-population--.intro: The parent named the three downstream probes and said what each one showed. This level takes them apart: what gets multiplied by what, what gets subtracted from what, and how far each result can be pushed before the paper itself stops pushing.

chapters.title: Multiplying one direction out to the vocabulary
chapters.body:
A feature is a unit vector $\mathbf{d}_i$ in the 512-dimensional space of MLP activations ([[feature-direction]]). Asking what it does to the output means pushing that vector through everything the model does after the MLP. In this model that is a short list.

[[mlp-output-weights|$W_{down}$]] comes first, carrying the 512 dimensions back into the 128-dimensional residual stream.

Then layer norm, which is where a linear trace would normally stop, because the normalization depends on the very activation it is applied to. The paper substitutes two fixed matrices: $\pi$, a projection that removes the mean, and $L$, a diagonal matrix standing in for the scaling terms ([[layer-norm-linearization]]). Both are held constant rather than recomputed per token.

Then [[unembedding-matrix|$W_{unembed}$]], out to one logit per vocabulary entry.

The product $\mathbf{d}_i W_{down} \pi L W_{unembed}$ is a single vector with one number per token. That is the feature's [[logit-weight]], and the recipe is [[path-expansion-logit-attribution|path expansion]] borrowed from the transformer circuits framework: expand the network into a sum of paths, read off one path, ignore the rest.

Notice what is absent from the product. The feature's activation never enters. The vector is the effect per unit of activation, which stands for the feature only because in the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] the MLP writes almost straight to the logits, so the effect scales with the activation instead of changing shape ([[linear-logit-effects]]).

One more adjustment. Adding a constant to every logit leaves the softmax unchanged, so these numbers have no absolute zero. The paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]).

After that, promoting a token always means promoting it relative to the typical vocabulary entry.

chapters.title: The shape that keeps recurring, and the one that does not
chapters.body:
Plotting that vector as a histogram — one count per vocabulary entry — is what the paper actually looks at.

One filtering choice comes first. Weights for extremely rare or never-used vocabulary entries are dropped, which the paper likens to the anomalous tokens others have reported, such as `SolidGoldMagikarp`. So the histogram is over a trimmed vocabulary, not the whole of it.

The shape has two parts. A tall mode sits at zero and covers nearly every token. The paper reads that mode as [[interference]]: with more feature directions than dimensions, directions cannot all be orthogonal, so a feature has small nonzero effects on tokens it has nothing to do with. Far to the right sits a small second mode ([[logit-weight-second-mode]]).

For the [[arabic-script-feature]] that second mode is Arabic characters together with the byte tokens `\xd8` and `\xd9` ([[fig-10]]). Those two appear because the tokenizer splits non-Latin characters into bytes, and these lead most characters in the basic Arabic block ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]). Promoting a script means promoting its lead bytes.

The [[dna-feature]] gives the same shape, its right mode made of nucleotide combinations like AGT and GCC ([[fig-22]]). The [[hebrew-feature]] gives it too, carrying `\xd7`.

The [[base64-feature]] is the exception ([[fig-26]]). Its tokens shade continuously from ordinary text into base64-specific rather than separating into two groups.

The paper's explanation is about the category, not the method. Whether a token belongs to Arabic script is close to a binary fact. Whether a token belongs to base64 is graded: `fr` is a base64 token and a common abbreviation for French, so the model has reason to be cautious about raising it, and any string of English letters has some genuine probability inside a base64 string.

The clean two-mode reading is therefore partly a property of how sharply the context cuts the vocabulary.

chapters.title: Three ways the linear picture could flatter a feature
chapters.body:
The paper lists the failure modes itself ([[logit-weight-caveats]]).

First, size. The [[logit-weight]] is per unit of activation and median-centred, so nothing in the histogram says how far the output actually moves once the vector is multiplied by a realistic [[feature-activation]]. Output weights small enough, and the second mode is genuine but inert.

Second, conditioning. A feature might fire only in contexts where other features have already driven those tokens to near-impossible, in which case pushing them up changes little. This is not hypothetical: elsewhere the paper says the model may simply not care what a feature does to tokens already suppressed by the [[direct-path]], the attention layer, or other features of the MLP.

Third, the layer norm approximation could be poor.

The paper's reply to all three is that the causal analysis which follows confirms the logit weight effects, so it does not believe the issues arise in practice. That is agreement between two methods, not a bound on the error of either.

One number does cover the population. In the [[automated-interpretability]] setup a language model writes an explanation of a unit from examples where it fires, and is then asked, given only that explanation, whether an unseen token is one the unit should predict as likely to come next. Scoring is against a 50/50 mix of top positive logit tokens and random other tokens, so guessing gives 50%.

Features average 74%. The transformer's own neurons average 58% ([[fig-41]]).

The [[randomized-transformer]] control scores at chance here, and the paper says plainly that this is unsurprising given weights that were shuffled. On this particular probe the control comes close to free.

chapters.title: Subtracting one direction and finishing the pass
chapters.body:
Run a context up to the MLP. Encode each token's activation into feature activations. At every token $j$, replace $\mathbf{x}^j$ with $\mathbf{x}^j - f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)\mathbf{d}_i$ ([[eq-feature-ablation]]). Then finish the forward pass and record the change in predicted log-likelihood of every token ([[feature-ablation]]).

Two things about that subtraction. It is applied across the whole context at once rather than at one position. And it removes a component, not a unit: zeroing a neuron would delete everything that neuron carried, which under [[superposition]] is several features at once, whereas subtracting $f_i\mathbf{d}_i$ deletes exactly what this one feature wrote ([[directional-ablation]]).

It is still approximate. The dictionary columns ([[dictionary-decoder]]) are not orthogonal to one another, so removing one perturbs the reconstruction of the rest a little.

Reading the display takes care, because the activation and the effect land on different tokens. An orange background says the feature fired there. An underline says how that token's own prediction changed. A feature active on B whose removal costs probability on C puts the background on B and the underline on C ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]).

The colours are worth taking from the figure's key rather than the prose: inside one section the paper names them blue and red in the convention sentence, then purple and orange two paragraphs later.

The Arabic result is that ablation hurt the prediction of every Arabic-script token and helped only the period, punctuation shared with other scripts ([[fig-11]]). The right-hand column draws from a band where the selected token fires at about half the left column's activation ([[activation-interval]]), and the effect survives there, visibly weaker.

That is ten displayed contexts, five per band, with no fitted relationship between activation and damage. The paper notes that computing ablation effects for every feature over every datapoint would be expensive, which is why they live per feature in the [[feature-exploration-interface]] rather than as a population number.

chapters.title: Seven rows, one sample each
chapters.body:
The asymmetry is the point. Ablation asks what a behaviour already underway loses when a feature is taken out. Pinning asks whether the feature can start a behaviour that nothing in the prompt calls for ([[pinned-feature-sampling]]).

Mechanically it is the ablation machinery run backwards. Encode the MLP activation into feature activations. Overwrite one coordinate with a high constant instead of the value the encoder produced. Decode, finish the pass, sample a token, repeat. The clamp is reapplied at every step of generation rather than set once.

For the Arabic panel the pinned value was that feature's maximum observed activation ([[fig-12]]). For the seven-row panel the paper says only "a fixed high number".

The panel itself ([[fig-43]]) is a control row plus seven interventions, all sampled at temperature $0.5$. The untouched model continues the counting prefix with `,8,30,20,8,10,10`, which does not even count correctly, and the paper says so in the same breath: one layer, very weak.

The rest are named in the paper's [[feature-notation]], drawn from the 4,096-feature run [[dictionary-learning-run|A/1]]. DNA, A/1/2937, gives `AGACCAGAGAGAGACAGAGAGAGGG`. The [[hexadecimal-feature]], A/1/3817, gives `E9D9A0C1C2C3`. Uppercase, A/1/3405, gives `USING IN THE UNITED STATES`. Han Chinese, Hebrew, Arabic and base64 fill the remaining rows.

What is claimed is the category of the output, not that any of it means anything. One Arabic sample carries a replacement glyph where the byte tokens failed to compose a character.

The seven were chosen the way section 3's four were, for being easy to name and easy to check ([[cherry-picked-case-studies]]). Section 4.3 does say pinned sampling was run across features and that the text matched the interpretation, but for that it points at the browser rather than a score. The weight of the [[feature-downstream-effects]] case sits on the other two probes.

n-the-same-features-twice--two-vectors-d.title: Reading the histogram entry by entry
n-the-same-features-twice--two-vectors-d.intro: The level above read one histogram off the page. This one asks where the numbers on its axis came from: which matrices produce them, which single step in that product is an approximation, which parts of the picture are conventions rather than measurements, and whether the same two-humped shape appears when the identical calculation is pointed at other features and at a neuron.

chapters.title: One chain of matrices
chapters.body:
The logit weight is never measured by running the model. It is read off the weights, by multiplying four matrices together.

Start where the feature lives. [[dictionary-learning]] here runs on the MLP activation vector of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], which has 512 dimensions. A feature's direction is therefore a vector $d_i$ in that 512-dimensional space — a column of the autoencoder's decoder. When the feature fires with activation $a_i$, the reconstruction contributes $a_i d_i$ to the MLP activations.

Now follow that vector forward. $W_{down}$, the [[mlp-output-weights]], maps the 512 MLP dimensions back down into the 128-dimensional [[residual-stream]]. A final layer norm follows, stood in for by a projection $\pi$ that removes the mean and a diagonal matrix $L$ that supplies the scaling. Then the [[unembedding-matrix]] $W_{unembed}$ turns those 128 numbers into one logit per vocabulary token.

Written out, the whole path is $d_i W_{down} \pi L W_{unembed}$.

The result is a row vector with one entry per vocabulary token. Each entry says how much one unit of this feature's activation moves that token's logit.

Nothing in that product depends on the context. That is what doing the calculation in weight space buys. The technique is [[path-expansion-logit-attribution]], taken from the transformer circuits framework: decompose the model's output into a sum over routes through the network, then read one route on its own.

A one-layer model has few routes. There is the [[direct-path]] from embedding straight to unembedding, the attention path, and the MLP path. The feature sits on the MLP path, and every step after the MLP on that path is linear once the layer norm is fixed ([[linear-logit-effects]]).

So the feature's contribution to the logits is the [[logit-weight]] scaled by the activation. One vector stands for what firing does. That is what lets [[feature-downstream-effects]] open with a weight calculation instead of an intervention.

chapters.title: The one step that is not exact
chapters.body:
Layer norm is the only nonlinearity standing between the MLP output and the logits. It is also the only part of that product that is approximated, so it is the step to look at closely.

Layer norm does three things. It subtracts the mean across the residual dimensions. It divides by the standard deviation of that same vector. Then it applies a learned per-dimension gain.

Two of the three are already linear. Subtracting the mean is a projection removing the all-ones direction, which is what $\pi$ is; nothing there is approximated. The learned gain is a diagonal matrix, so it is exact as well.

The division is the problem. That denominator is a single scalar computed from the whole residual vector at that token position. It changes from token to token. It even depends on the feature's own contribution, since the feature writes into the vector being normalised.

The paper freezes it. A representative scale is folded into the diagonal $L$ and treated as constant ([[layer-norm-linearization]]).

What this buys is the rest of the analysis: one fixed vector per feature, identical across every context, which can be histogrammed ([[logit-weight-histogram]]) and correlated against another model's. What it costs is that the number is no longer exactly what happens at any particular token.

The paper names this as one of three [[logit-weight-caveats]]. The other two are not about the approximation at all. The weights might be real but too small to matter once multiplied by typical activations. Or the feature might fire only where other contributions have already driven those tokens' logits down, so raising them changes little.

No error bound is offered for any of the three. What is offered instead is agreement from two checks that do run the model: [[feature-ablation]] and [[pinned-feature-sampling]]. The paper's own wording is that, based on the subsequent analysis, it does not believe these issues arise in practice. That is corroboration rather than measurement, and it is strongest where activations are large ([[large-activations-dominate]]).

chapters.title: Two things on the plot are conventions
chapters.body:
Add the same constant $c$ to every next-token logit. In $e^{z_k+c}/\sum_j e^{z_j+c}$ the factor $e^c$ appears above and below, and cancels. The distribution is unchanged.

So a feature's [[logit-weight]] vector, and that vector plus a constant, describe the same behaviour. The offset carries no information. Before plotting anything you have to pick one, and the pick is yours.

Notice what is not free. Multiplying every entry by two doubles a real difference between two tokens, which would be a different model. Only the offset is arbitrary. On the histogram, the width of the bulk and the distance out to the second mode are measurements; where either mode sits on the axis is not.

Given a free offset, why the median ([[logit-weight-median-centering]])? Because the bulk mode holds nearly the whole vocabulary, so the median falls inside it, and centering there puts the bulk at zero. The mean would not. The mean is pulled right by the far tail, by an amount depending on how many tokens are in the second mode — the very quantity the plot exists to show.

The second convention is which entries get plotted at all. The vocabulary comes from [[byte-pair-encoding]], so it holds byte-level entries and merges that the [[pile-dataset]] barely exercises. An unembedding row that training never pushed in any consistent direction still holds some value. Dotting a feature's residual direction into that row still returns a number, occasionally a large one.

That number is not behaviour. The paper drops those entries, likening them to the anomalous tokens of Rumbelow and Watkins ([[anomalous-token-exclusion]]).

Two things follow. An arbitrary entry could land near $0.5$ and get labelled in the inset of [[fig-10]], exactly where the reading of the [[arabic-script-feature]] is most delicate. And enough such entries would shift the median, so the filter has to run before the centering.

The paper gives no cutoff for "extremely rare". The filter is taken on trust.

chapters.title: The same shape, three more times
chapters.body:
The claim that this shape recurs is cheap to make and worth checking against the cases where it had no reason to come easily.

The [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937 gives one. Its logit weights have the same profile, and the tokens in the far mode are nucleotide triples: AGT, GCC and their neighbours ([[fig-22]]). Nothing in that mode is a Unicode effect. So the two humps are not an artifact of how non-Latin scripts get tokenised.

The [[hebrew-feature]] A/1/416 gives another, and this one does run through tokenisation. Its far mode holds Hebrew letters plus the byte token `\xd7`, which begins the UTF-8 encoding of most characters in the basic Hebrew block ([[fig-34]]). Same lead-byte logic as Arabic, different script, same picture ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

Then the second transformer. B is trained on the same data with the same hyperparameters and a different random seed, and gets its own separately trained dictionary ([[transformer-a-and-b]]). B's base64 counterpart shows a small second mode in the same place ([[fig-28]]). So does its Hebrew counterpart ([[fig-37]]). Reseeding does not remove the shape.

The check that carries the most weight is the negative one. Run the identical calculation on a neuron. A/neurons/489 is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] for the Arabic feature, and its logit weights form a single mode ([[fig-15]]). The Arabic tokens are a thin red sliver inside the bulk, leaning very slightly positive, with some of them negative.

That matters because it rules out the plotting pipeline as the cause. Path expansion does not hand back two humps for whatever direction you point it at. The [[logit-weight-second-mode]] is a property of these particular directions, not of the procedure that draws them.

chapters.title: Where the two humps blur
chapters.body:
One case study does not produce the clean gap, and the paper says so.

For the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 the far mode is there, but the approach to it is a gradient rather than a cliff ([[fig-26]]). The right-hand side of the main mode is already skewed towards tokens that are base64-neutral or slightly base64-leaning. The narrow conditional strip drawn beneath the histogram shades continuously from ordinary text tokens into base64-specific ones.

The paper's explanation is about the world, not the method. Whether a token belongs to Arabic script is close to a binary fact, and the [[arabic-script-proxy]] can settle it from Unicode blocks alone. Whether a token belongs to base64 is not binary at all. Any string of English letters has some chance of turning up inside a base64 blob.

The paper's example is 'fr', which is a base64 substring and also a common abbreviation for French. Pushing 'fr' up hard would cost the model whenever the context is French. Pushing it up a little is the right amount. The gradation in the histogram is the model hedging, sensibly.

One further caution comes with this figure. The colouring is less reliable here too. The [[base64-proxy]] treats base64 as random draws over the characters `a`–`z`, `A`–`Z`, `0`–`9`, `+` and `/`, which is broad enough to fire on hexadecimal strings that have a feature of their own ([[hexadecimal-feature]]), and its correlation with the feature's activations is only $0.38$. A blurred picture therefore has two candidate causes at once, and it is easy to blame the wrong one.

The paper's later evaluations still treat the far mode as legible. The [[feature-interpretability-rubric]] awards a point when inconsistent positive logits are at least clearly smaller than the consistent ones ([[rubric-effect-size-separation]]) — an item written for exactly this blurred case. And in [[automated-logit-scoring]], Claude gets a feature's written explanation and judges whether an unseen high-logit token is one that feature should predict: 74% across features against 58% across neurons, on a 50/50 mix where chance is 50% ([[fig-41]]).

Readable enough to grade. Not always cleanly split.

n-what-the-collection-looks-like--featur.title: Four nodes, and one it cannot reach
n-what-the-collection-looks-like--featur.intro: The parent gave the four HTML states and the four IRC states as lists of tokens. This level opens each box: what the feature actually fires on, how long the promoted-token lists really are, what kind of evidence an arrow label is, what would have to happen after ` href`, and why the paper thinks the two systems claiming the same bracket are not just an artifact of its own method.

chapters.title: The four states, spelled out
chapters.body:
Each box in [[fig-58]] has two sides, and the figure draws both.

The input side is a stack of dataset examples. Orange shading marks the tokens where the feature fires, darker for a larger [[feature-activation]], with four tokens of context on each side of the sampled one ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]).

The output side is the arrow leaving the box. Its label is the top of the feature's [[logit-weight]] vector — one number per vocabulary token, saying how much this feature firing raises that token's next-token logit. Naming a feature by what it promotes rather than what it answers to is the [[action-features]] reading, and this whole diagram depends on it.

Now the states at full resolution.

A/0/20 does not fire on `<` alone. Its shaded tokens include `</`, `><` and `></`. Under [[feature-notation]] the A names the transformer and the 0 names the [[dictionary-learning-run]]; the 20 is only where training happened to put this unit.

A/0/0 fires on tag names, hardest on ul, then li, div, nav, entry. Its promoted list is longer than the parent's four: `>`, `></`, `/>`, `><`, and `>` fused to punctuation — `>,` `>.` `>&` `>)` `>;` `>/`.

A/0/30 fires on that `>` or `/>`. It promotes three different whitespace tokens: a newline with four spaces, a newline with eight, a newline with two. The state is a family of indent depths, not one token.

A/0/494 fires on any of them. Its list is ` <`, ` </`, ` <!--`, `</` — an element opening, an element closing, and a comment opening.

So "back to the start" is really three different HTML constructs sharing one state. The node-by-node summary sits at [[html-feature-automaton]].

chapters.title: Seven arrows, and what a label is
chapters.body:
Count the labels and their lengths: nine tokens, ten, three, four, two, two, three. Those are truncated tops of lists, not complete vectors. The real [[logit-weight]] has one entry per vocabulary item, and the figure prints whatever fits above an arrow.

The two short labels are the shortcuts. From A/0/0 back to A/0/20: `></` and `><`. From A/0/30 back to A/0/20: ` </` and ` />`.

The mechanism is the byte-pair vocabulary. A closing bracket followed immediately by an opening bracket is common enough in HTML that the tokenizer merged the pair into a single vocabulary item. Emitting that item crosses two of the drawn states in one step, so the whitespace node never gets a turn.

The shape of the machine is therefore partly a fact about the vocabulary rather than about the markup language ([[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]]). The same force works the other way elsewhere in this section, where split characters force extra states into existence rather than letting states be skipped ([[unicode-token-state-machines]]).

One thing the arrows are not: measured transitions.

Nobody sampled from the model and counted how often `></` actually follows a tag name. The label is a ranked list, median-centred so it carries no absolute scale ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]), with never-used vocabulary entries dropped before ranking ([[anomalous-token-exclusion]]).

And the paper states three separate ways this linear quantity can overstate a feature's real effect on the output ([[logit-weight-caveats]]). Every arrow here inherits all three. The system is read off token rankings, and that is the whole of the evidence for it.

chapters.title: The exit nothing covers
chapters.body:
Work out what the dashed arrow would need. Suppose the model emits ` href`.

What follows is `=`, then a quote, then a URL that may run for many tokens, then a closing quote. Then either whitespace and a second attribute name, or the `>` that finally ends the tag.

That is at least three more states, and one of them — the URL interior — is a span rather than a single token, so it would need a feature of the kind that stays on across a region. None of the four features in the figure fires anywhere in that stretch.

Why the picture is this small is not a mystery. A/0 learns 512 dictionary units for the 512-neuron MLP of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], an [[expansion-factor]] of exactly one, so the dictionary is not overcomplete ([[overcompleteness]]).

The paper's premise is that the layer packs more features than it has neurons ([[superposition]]). A dictionary with one unit per neuron therefore cannot be recovering all of them. It is a summary at the coarsest available zoom ([[dictionary-resolution]]), and the paper says the same material in A/1, eight times wider, would look far more complex as each node divides ([[feature-splitting]]).

But coarseness and incompleteness are different complaints, and it is worth being exact about which one the gap shows.

The missing attribute states do not show that the model lacks the machinery. They show that these four units do not carry it. Nothing in the paper reports a search of A/0 for an attribute-value feature that came back empty.

So the honest reading is narrow: the figure is a hand-assembled illustration, not a decomposition of everything A/0 knows about HTML, and the distance between a dictionary's units and the model's own [[true-features]] is exactly what stays open here.

chapters.title: Four states for one chat line
chapters.body:
[[fig-59]] carves a single line of chat into four, and each node is more particular than its label.

A/0/178 fires on the `<` that opens a nickname, and the examples all show it directly after a line break. It promotes handle openers as subword pieces: ubottu, vin, dan, baz, nick, gunt, lu, dav, Blues, Dr. The first of those is the name of a well-known Ubuntu support bot.

A/0/153 shades the whole nick interior, digits included — Porkepix2, Adam-85, jnoob22. So it tracks the bracketed span rather than any word. Its self-loop tokens are `_`, `ix`, `onia`, `oy`, `oke`, `fer`, `ob`, `gi`; `ob` recurs because handles ending in noob are common here. It also promotes `>` and `_>`, the second of which is one token covering an underscore and a bracket together.

A/0/151 fires most strongly on that `>`. It also fires weakly on the addressed-nick colon: mgolisch:, nibbler_:, Adam-85:. That makes the state closer to "a message is about to begin" than to "a closing bracket". It promotes nine openers — " hmm", " yeah", " hey", " ok", " hello", " heh", " yep", " ah", " lol".

A/0/46 shades entire message lines, including ordinary words like "on" and "given", and switches off at the line break. That behaviour makes it one of the [[context-features]] rather than a topic detector.

The two self-loops are what buy unbounded length ([[self-exciting-feature-loop]]). A feature that fixed a short continuation ([[trigram-features]]) could not let a handle run as long as it likes.

So these four nodes straddle two of the paper's [[feature-motifs]]: two single-token states and two span states. The Ubuntu vocabulary on the last one is presumed to come from the [[pile-dataset]].

chapters.title: Why the same bracket picks a different feature
chapters.body:
The mechanism is not mysterious. The autoencoder reads the MLP activation at one position, and that activation is computed from the residual stream there, which the attention layer has already mixed with earlier tokens.

So a dictionary unit can be a conjunction: this token is `<`, and the preceding text looks like markup. The paper's own footnote says MLP layers are well positioned to compute exactly such conjunctions, which is its explanation for how many [[token-in-context-features]] it keeps finding.

Token identity does not select the feature. The residual stream does.

The harder question is whether the transformer really works this way. Put it as [[local-vs-compositional-codes]]: a [[local-code]] spends one unit per token-and-context pair, while a [[compositional-code]] would keep one `<` unit and combine it with a separate HTML unit or IRC unit.

Local codes are sparser. The [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] rewards sparsity. So the method has a standing incentive to manufacture the very thing being observed ([[are-token-in-context-features-real]]).

The paper's counterargument applies cleanly to these two figures ([[sharper-predictions-argument]]). Under a compositional code, the logits after `<` would have to be a sum: tokens that generally follow a bracket, plus tokens generally common in this context.

Now compare the lists. A/0/20 promotes div, td, thead. A/0/178 promotes ubottu, dav, Blues. The overlap is close to nothing, which a sum could only reproduce if the bracket term were nearly flat — and a nearly flat term is a term doing no work.

That is an argument, not a measurement, and the paper only claims the local reading holds "to some extent".

One last note on why this matters for units. A single neuron carrying both jobs would read as [[polysemanticity]]; here they are two units, and both can be pulled up by index in the [[feature-exploration-interface]].

n-what-the-collection-looks-like--wideni.title: One number for linking two dictionaries
n-what-the-collection-looks-like--wideni.intro: The summary above named the measure and its two stated choices. Here we do the algebra that makes masking necessary, put numbers on what a symmetric score would have returned, and read the graph box by box — including the one box that breaks the tree.

chapters.title: Zeros are free, so the mask is doing something else
chapters.body:
Start from how sparse these activations are. A live feature in [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/1 — the paper's [[feature-notation]] for one trained [[sparse-autoencoder]] — typically has a [[feature-density]] near one token in $10^5$. Sample a few million tokens and its vector of [[feature-activation]] values is almost entirely zeros.

Now notice what those zeros cost in a cosine similarity. A token where both features are silent adds nothing to the dot product, and nothing to either norm. So the unmasked cosine over all sampled tokens is already the same number as the cosine over the union of the two firing sets.

The mask is therefore not there to strip out shared silence. Restricting to $S_a$ leaves the numerator untouched, because outside $S_a$ the first feature is zero anyway. What it changes is the denominator: the second feature's norm shrinks to only the mass it has on $S_a$. Masking divides out however much the other feature does elsewhere.

Walk it with round numbers. Let a fine feature fire at value $1$ on $1{,}000$ tokens, and a coarse feature fire at value $1$ on $10{,}000$ tokens including all $1{,}000$ of them. The dot product is $1{,}000$, the fine norm is $\sqrt{1000}\approx 31.6$, the coarse norm is $100$.

Unmasked, that is $1000/(31.6\times 100)\approx 0.32$. Masked to the fine feature's tokens the coarse norm drops to $31.6$, giving $1000/(31.6\times 31.6)=1.0$. Masked to the coarse feature's tokens nothing changes and you get $0.32$ again.

So perfect containment — the exact shape [[feature-splitting]] predicts — scores $0.32$ symmetrically. That is below the threshold [[masked-cosine-similarity]] uses, and it falls further as the coarse feature's territory widens.

chapters.title: What taking the maximum buys, and what it discards
chapters.body:
The two masked numbers in that example were $1.0$ and $0.32$. Keeping the larger makes the score a test for containment without needing to know in advance which feature is the narrow one.

But the discarded number was the informative one. The gap between the two masks is what says which direction the containment runs. Once you keep only the maximum, the score cannot distinguish "the first refines the second" from "the second refines the first", nor either from "these are the same feature seen twice".

The graph gets that direction from its layout instead. Columns are ordered by dictionary width, so the arrow of refinement is an assumption about the sweep, not a reading off the measure.

It is also worth being clear about which kind of similarity this is. The paper has a geometric notion available: each feature has a [[feature-direction]], a decoder column, and conceptually related features turn out to sit at small angles — that is [[feature-geometry-clusters]], visible in the [[feature-umap]] of [[fig-44]]. [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]], the measure other [[dictionary-learning|dictionary-learning]] work reports, compares dictionaries that way, by their vectors. The splitting graph does not. It compares when features fire, not where they point.

The paper also had a second measure already in hand. For [[universality]] it matches a feature in A/1 to its counterpart in B/1 by [[activation-similarity]] — a plain [[pearson-correlation]] over datapoints, with no mask and no maximum, median $0.72$.

The difference in treatment fits the different job. Across two dictionaries of equal width the expected relation is one-to-one; across widths it is containment. The paper does not spell that reasoning out. Note too that a correlation subtracts a mean and a cosine does not, so the two are not interchangeable even before masking.

chapters.title: The threshold and the filter are both choices about the picture
chapters.body:
The paper is candid that $0.4$ was chosen to balance a graph small enough to visualize against showing some of the richness of splitting. That makes the number of edges a display parameter. Turn it down and the figure thickens; turn it up and branches disappear.

Nothing calibrates the value. There is no null distribution for what [[masked-cosine-similarity]] does on unrelated features, and no shuffled-activation control. The paper builds controls of that kind elsewhere — a [[randomized-transformer]] via [[weight-shuffling]] gives a baseline for interpretability scores — but not here.

And $0.4$ is loose against the arithmetic above. Genuine containment scored $1.0$; a bar at $0.4$ admits pairs that agree only moderately on the narrower feature's own territory. The drawn edge shows that a pair cleared the bar, not by how much, so a link at $0.41$ and a link at $0.95$ look the same.

The second choice is the exclusion. In A/1, of $4{,}096$ learned features, $168$ are dead — active on none of $100$ million examples — and $292$ more fire on fewer than one token in a million. That second group is the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], about $7\%$ of the dictionary, and it is the left mode of the [[feature-density-histogram]].

The modes behave differently. Almost every feature in the right mode, the [[high-density-cluster]], is anecdotally interpretable; almost none in the left mode are. Where the two overlap, [[density-cluster-separation]] pulls them apart using the bias and the encoder–decoder dot product.

These are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]: a zero-activity count for [[dead-neurons]] misses them entirely. The exclusion is applied across the whole paper, not invented for this graph. One further reason applies here specifically, though the paper does not give it — on a support of a handful of tokens, a restricted cosine near $1$ is cheap.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

chapters.title: Three widths, twenty boxes, and one check that isn't a label
chapters.body:
The columns of [[fig-46]] hold $512$, $4{,}096$ and $16{,}384$ features. The MLP of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] is $512$ neurons wide, so those are [[expansion-factor]]s of $1\times$, $8\times$ and $32\times$. The [[l1-coefficient]] is held fixed across the three, so width is the only difference.

The figure traces two coarse features into seven and then eleven. A small discrepancy is worth noticing: the surrounding text says the coarsest run has three features for technical settings, while the printed graph follows two.

Follow the purple branch. A/0/341 is "the" in mathematical prose, a [[token-in-context-features]] case — one token, one kind of surrounding text. In A/1 its territory is covered by "the" in machine learning, "the" in topology and complex analysis, and "a" in math. In A/2 the topology feature divides again, into complex analysis and topology-with-abstract-algebra.

The "a" branch splits on something other than subject. Its two A/2 children separate "a" as a variable inside equations from "a" as the article in prose.

All of that is read off human descriptions of what each box fires on. The one check that does not depend on the descriptions is the [[logit-weight]] — computed from the weights along the [[direct-path]], not from anyone's reading.

It moves the same way. The coarse A/0/341 supports generic completions: *the denominator*, *the remainder*, *the theorem*. A/2/15021 supports *the dataset* and *the classifier*; A/2/4878 supports *the quotient* and *the subgroup*; A/2/2609 supports *the gauge*, *the Lagrangian*, *the spacetime*.

That is four features and their top few entries, with no score attached. The figure's own caption for A/2/2609 says prepositions in physics and technical writing, while the text calls it gravitation and field theory.

chapters.title: The box that stops it being a tree
chapters.body:
One box in the graph receives edges of both colours. A/1/512 — "a" in the context of math — descends from A/0/341, the mathematical "the", and also from A/0/281, a feature for abstract algebra terminology and notation.

So widening the dictionary is not subdividing cells of a partition. A narrow feature can sit under two coarse ones at once, because the coarse ones overlap on its territory and each clears the threshold against it.

Be clear about how much carries this. It is one box out of the twenty drawn, and the merge exists only relative to the $0.4$ bar — a higher bar could have removed one of the two parent edges. The paper states the general claim, that features may both split and merge, from this example.

The consequence for the summary picture is real even so. [[dictionary-resolution]] survives as zoom level and dies as taxonomy. If there is some fixed set of [[true-features]] underneath, the wider run is not carving up the coarse feature; it is re-covering the same region of activation space with more and narrower directions, and coverage can overlap where a partition could not.

That overlap is what a [[local-vs-compositional-codes]] reading would predict: "a in math" shares territory with both "math notation" and "the in math", so both partly claim it.

Practically, you cannot walk this graph the way you walk a hierarchy. A fine feature has no single parent, which is part of why the paper doubts there is a [[correct-number-of-features]] to aim at. The [[feature-relationship-graph]] and [[splitting-is-not-a-tree]] pages carry the rest, and [[multiple-features-for-one-context]] shows what the same overlap looks like from inside a single run.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--densi.title: Dead, alive, and the third thing
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--densi.intro: The parent gave you the shape of the argument: a revival mechanism, a population that slips past it, and two readings of what that population is. This level supplies the parts that decide the argument — the exact schedule and window the check uses, the six-step procedure that brings a unit back, the arithmetic at the scale the check actually runs on, and what the outside replication reports in enough detail to see where it disagrees.

chapters.title: The check, and when it runs
chapters.body:
The detection rule has two parts, a schedule and a window, and both do work.

The schedule is four fixed points: training steps 25,000, 50,000, 75,000 and 100,000. [[neuron-resampling]] runs at those steps and at no others. Training the [[sparse-autoencoder]] takes 1,000,000 update steps at a batch size of 8,192, drawn from the [[autoencoder-training-dataset]].

So every revival the run will ever perform happens inside the first tenth of training.

A unit that stops firing at step 300,000 is never brought back. It sits in the dictionary, contributing nothing, for the remaining seven hundred thousand steps.

The window is the test itself. At each of the four checkpoints, the code asks which units have not fired in *any* of the previous 12,500 steps. At 8,192 vectors per step, that window covers 102.4 million activation vectors — each drawn from a different context by [[activation-shuffling]], and none of them repeated, since the run uses [[sampling-without-replacement]].

So [[dead-neurons]] here has a concrete meaning: a unit that returned exactly zero across a hundred million consecutive inputs.

The paper also lists what drives units into that state — learning rate too high, batch size too low, redundancy in the data (too many tokens taken per context, or repeated epochs), too many training steps, and the choice of optimizer. The list is offered without measurements, as things the authors observed.

One entry on it is worth holding onto. "Too many training steps" kills units, while the separate advice from the [[learning-rate-sweep]] is that a lower learning rate with more steps finds more real features, and [[extended-training-steps]] is listed among the changes that mattered most. The same knob appears on both lists.

Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

chapters.title: Seeding a revived unit
chapters.body:
Reinitializing a dead unit at random would waste it: it would land somewhere the autoencoder already reconstructs adequately and die again. The procedure instead aims each revived unit at a datapoint the current model handles worst.

It runs in six steps.

First, compute the autoencoder's loss on a random subset of 819,200 inputs — a hundred batches' worth. Second, assign each input a probability of being drawn proportional to the *square* of that loss, not to the loss itself; squaring concentrates the draw further into the tail of badly reconstructed inputs. This is [[loss-proportional-input-sampling]], and the paper states the intent without arguing for the exponent.

Third, for each dead unit, draw one input under those probabilities and renormalize it to unit L2 norm. That vector becomes the unit's column in the [[dictionary-decoder]] — its [[feature-direction]] — which is consistent with the standing constraint of [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]].

Fourth, the [[autoencoder-encoder]] row gets the same direction, but scaled to 0.2 times the average encoder norm across the units still alive, with its bias element set to zero. That is [[resampled-encoder-scaling]], and it is the part the paper insists on. A revived unit at full encoder strength would start writing into the reconstruction immediately, disturbing every feature sharing that region of activation space — [[interference]]. At a fifth of the usual norm it fires only weakly, and only for inputs close to its seed.

Fifth, [[adam-state-reset-on-resampling]]: the moment estimates for every changed weight and bias are cleared, since they describe a unit that no longer exists.

The paper reports this beating both no resampling and a plain [[kaiming-uniform-initialization]] reset. It also reports the costs plainly. Each resampling event produces a sudden loss spike, and resampling more often than this makes training diverge. Better strategies are called an open problem; the [[lottery-ticket-hypothesis]] is offered only as a possible reason it helps at all.

chapters.title: Why the spike survives the check
chapters.body:
The arithmetic the parent walked was over the whole run. The arithmetic that decides the outcome is over one window.

A [[feature-density]] of $10^{-7}$ means firing on one token in ten million. The check window holds $1.024 \times 10^{8}$ activation vectors. Divide: the expected number of firings in a single window is about ten.

Treat firings as independent and the chance of a window with none is $e^{-10.24}$, roughly four in a hundred thousand. Firings are not independent — a feature that fires does so on a whole stretch of one context, so silences clump and the true chance is higher than that. But the margin is not close. The test needs exactly zero, and the unit is delivering ten.

So the left spike of [[fig-64]] passes all four checks, and passes them comfortably. These are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]: dead by any standard that cares what a dictionary slot is for, alive by the standard the code applies.

Catching them would take a window a thousand times longer than the run allows, or a different rule altogether — a density threshold rather than a zero test. Neither is what the paper implemented.

The consequence lands on how you count. A raw tally of units that fired at least once counts the whole [[ultralow-density-cluster]] as features found, and in a run with a large [[expansion-factor]] and a large [[l1-coefficient]] that cluster can be most of the dictionary. This is exactly why the paper's headline number off a [[feature-density-histogram]] is the count of units in the [[high-density-cluster]] rather than the count of units alive; the reasoning behind that choice is [[feature-density-diagnostics]].

chapters.title: The case that they are an artifact
chapters.body:
Of the two observations, the training-length one carries the weight, and it is worth being exact about why.

The transformer is frozen. Its weights were fixed before a single activation vector was collected, and nothing the autoencoder's optimizer does can change them. So if a property of the ultralow mode can be made to shrink by running that optimizer longer, the property belongs to the fitting procedure and not to the model being fitted. That is the whole argument, and it is a clean one.

What happens mechanically fits the earlier list. Push training further and units drift out of the ultralow mode into genuine silence — which is the same event as "too many training steps produces dead units", seen from the other side. Past step 100,000 nothing revives them, so they simply stop being counted as features at all.

The evidence is thinner than the argument. The paper reports this in a sentence, with no figure, no counts, and no sweep over training length. A reader has to take it as stated.

The hedging is on the page too. The cluster *appears* to be an artifact of training; the source is under investigation; the authors want either a way to prevent these units or a way to detect and filter them automatically. Given how much of [[evaluating-dictionary-learning]] rests on density, that is an admission with teeth.

The other observation — that ultralow units resist [[manual-inspection]] while high-density ones do not — is weaker on its own, because "real, but not interpretable by us" would produce the same split.

The [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]] aside is weaker still, and marked as a suspicion. If many units in a [[dictionary-learning-run]] are near-copies of one direction, matching them against a second dictionary would give those matches a mode of their own. That would put a bimodality reported elsewhere in [[dictionary-learning]] down to a training artifact rather than to anything about [[feature]] structure. The paper does not test it.

chapters.title: The replication cuts back
chapters.body:
The outside comment in [[external-replication]] was trained on a different open-source one-layer GELU model, not on the paper's own [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. Two of its findings sit awkwardly against the artifact reading, and one detail undercuts the comparison itself.

Start with the detail. The replicator's cluster is defined as density below $10^{-4}$, while the paper's left mode sits near $10^{-7}$. That is three orders of magnitude, and the paper's own [[high-density-cluster]] would fall inside the replicator's threshold. The two "ultra-low clusters" may not name the same population. The replicator also found no fully dead features at all, where the paper found enough of them to build a revival procedure around.

Now the finding. More than half the features fell into that cluster, and nearly all of them shared one encoder direction — but not one decoder direction.

That asymmetry is the informative part. Under [[untied-decoder-weights]], the encoder row is the detector, the projection used to decide whether a feature is present, while the decoder column is what gets written back; both [[encoder-decoder-offset-crosstalk]] and the [[amortized-sparse-coding-approximation]] framing turn on the two doing different jobs. In the replication their median cosine similarity per feature was only 0.5. So this cluster looks like one detector duplicated across hundreds of units, each writing something different. On a single input, 95% of them fired at once — which is what a duplicated detector predicts, and what a set of genuinely distinct rare features does not.

The direction re-formed across random seeds. The replicator reads seed stability as a fact about the model, and reports failing to interpret what the direction was. Constraining a fresh autoencoder to be orthogonal to it produced a new cluster along a new direction — which reads either as the training dynamic reasserting itself, or as more structure of the same kind. Neither reading is settled here, and the paper prints the comment as received. On what makes a direction the model's own rather than the fitter's, see [[privileged-basis]], [[fig-63]] and [[superposition]].

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.title: Where the activations actually are
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.intro: The parent gave the shape of the argument: band the spectrum, find a drop-off at the weak end, answer it by weighting activations rather than counting tokens. This level opens each step — how a band is built and what its score is measured against, what the drop-off figure does and does not report, the arithmetic the re-weighting performs, and how much of the defence is an argument about a one-layer architecture rather than a measurement.

chapters.title: Eleven bands, and what each score is measured against
chapters.body:
Start with the construction. A feature's activation is a single non-negative number per token — the ReLU hidden unit of the autoencoder, written $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ and explained at [[feature-activation]].

Over a large sample of data, that feature has some maximum $M$. The annotator takes eleven levels evenly spaced from $0$ to $M$, and an [[activation-interval]] is the set of examples whose activation is closest to one of those levels.

Two things follow from spacing them that way. The bands are cut relative to each feature's own maximum, so the third band of one feature and the third band of another are not the same absolute activation. And within a band, examples are drawn uniformly, so a band of faint firings gets exactly as much of the annotator's attention as the band at the top.

Then the scoring, which is where the design does its real work. The annotator first forms one interpretation of the unit from everything — its positive logit effects and its activations across all eleven bands together. Only then is each band scored, against that single fixed hypothesis.

The bands are not judged on their own terms. That is the whole point. Read alone, almost any slice of a mixed unit looks coherent; what convicts it is a band that is coherent about something else.

This is the correction to [[max-dataset-example-bias]], the weakness the paper names in its own earlier work: reading only [[top-dataset-examples]] hides [[polysemanticity]] rather than testing for it. It also changes the unit of measurement in [[manual-interpretability-scoring]] — the thing that receives a [[feature-interpretability-rubric]] score is an interval, not a feature. The procedure is [[activation-interval-analysis]].

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

chapters.title: The shape of the drop-off, and the angle
chapters.body:
What comes back from that scoring is [[fig-42]], and it is worth being precise about what it reports.

Higher bands score more consistent with the feature's hypothesis than lower ones. The paper describes two patterns in the population: many features hold across the entire spectrum, and some hold across roughly the top 60% and then fall away quickly below it.

No split is given between those groups. "Many" and "some" are the paper's words, and no fraction of features is attached to either.

The suggested cause is worth unpacking before it is named. Suppose the direction the [[sparse-autoencoder]] learned is not quite the direction the model is using — the learned column sits at a small angle to the true [[feature-direction]].

The activation read off that column is a projection. When the true feature is firing hard, the projection is large and dominated by the true feature, because a small angle $\theta$ costs you only a factor of $\cos\theta$.

But a slightly-off direction also picks up other features. In an overcomplete dictionary the directions cannot all be perpendicular — see [[overcompleteness]] and the crosstalk it forces, [[interference]] — so other active features leak a little into the read-out.

That leakage does not scale with the true feature. It is roughly the same size whether the true feature is firing hard or faintly.

So at the weak end, leak and signal become comparable, and the band fills with a mixture. That is [[feature-at-slight-angle]], and it is the failure mode [[superposition]] would predict for an imperfectly recovered direction.

The paper offers it in one sentence, hedged: it says this is possible. No angles are measured, no correction is attempted, and no competing explanation is compared against it here.
