chapters.title: Counting tokens, weighting magnitudes
chapters.body:
The [[low-interval-activation-skew]] and the drop-off point in opposite directions, so the defence has to change what is being counted.

A plain activation histogram — the [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]] the paper uses throughout for [[activation-specificity]] — bins tokens by activation and makes each bar's height a token count. Every firing counts once, a faint one exactly as much as a maximal one.

An [[expected-value-plot]] keeps the bins and changes the height: a bar becomes the total activation contributed by the tokens in it, count times activation.

Walk one bin against another. A bin at activation $0.5$ holding a hundred tokens contributes $50$ of activation; a bin at $5$ holding twenty tokens contributes $100$. Counted by tokens, the first bin is five times the second. Weighted by magnitude, the second is twice the first.

The numbers for the [[arabic-script-feature]] come from a [[computational-proxy]], a per-token log likelihood ratio for Arabic script. Arabic is 0.13% of training tokens, and 81% of the tokens on which the feature fires at all. Split by strength in [[fig-8]], that 81% runs from 25% where the feature is barely on to 98% above an activation of 5. Re-weighted in [[fig-9]], almost all the activation mass sits in Arabic text.

Note what has just been substituted. The caveat in [[interpretability-evaluation-caveats]] is about the whole scored population of features and neurons. The answer offered to it is one figure, for one feature, taken from the case studies. The paper is explicit that this is where the reassurance comes from.

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron

chapters.title: What the weighting assumes
chapters.body:
Weighting by magnitude is the right move only if the model's behaviour scales with magnitude. That premise is [[large-activations-dominate]], and its support differs sharply inside and outside the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]].

Inside, the argument is architectural. A feature contributes its activation times its dictionary direction to the MLP output, that lands in the residual stream, and from there to the logits there is no further nonlinearity — only the rescaling of layer norm.

So the effect on the logits is close to linear in the activation. That is [[linear-logit-effects]], and it is also what makes a single [[logit-weight]] vector a well-defined summary of a feature's [[feature-downstream-effects]].

Run the arithmetic the weighting implies. A firing at $0.5$ shifts the logits about a tenth as far as a firing at $5$, so ten faint firings are worth roughly one strong one — precisely the exchange rate the [[expected-value-plot]] assumes.

Outside a one-layer model, the paper's own footnote gives three weaker supports and no more. It follows from conjectures and heuristic arguments — the abundance of linear pathways, the idea of linear features at each layer. It must hold for sufficiently small activations by continuity. And it does not have a watertight argument.

Continuity earns the limit at zero, not the middle of the range, which is where most of the firings sit.

This is the load-bearing step of the whole defence, the one that turns "most firings are weak and impure" into "and it does not matter much". Even in the testbed it is reasoned from architecture rather than measured: the paper does not report, say, a [[feature-ablation]] restricted to the weak firings alone.

chapters.title: Three readings of the weak end
chapters.body:
The impurity at low activations may not be a fact about the feature at all. The paper lists three candidates in [[weak-activation-hypotheses]] and does not choose between them.

First, [[proxy-false-negatives]]. The Arabic proxy scores tokens by Unicode block, and whitespace, punctuation and newlines live in other blocks, so a token sitting inside Arabic text can be scored as not Arabic. The [[dna-feature]] audit is the concrete version: in [[fig-21]] the disagreements between feature and proxy were read case by case, and in all but two the feature was right and the proxy wrong — the space in `TGG AGT`, or the `'-` in `5'-TCT`, where the feature fires on a prefix that is not itself DNA but is followed by DNA.

Second, [[calibrated-feature-activations]]. If a feature's activation tracks the model's confidence that some property holds, then weak activations are supposed to be wrong some of the time. The model here is one layer, and Unicode characters are often split across two byte tokens, so telling the script from a single token is genuinely uncertain. Under this reading the weak end is calibration rather than error — and the [[hebrew-feature]], which fires weakly on other Unicode-script languages, is the pattern you would expect.

Third, [[autoencoder-width-limitation]]. If the dictionary holds fewer directions than the model has features, the unrecovered ones do not vanish; they smear as small activations across many learned features.

That third reading is the expensive one. It says the weak end is real and the [[dictionary-learning]] run is too narrow — which is also what [[feature-splitting]] suggests, since widening the dictionary keeps turning up more structure in the same territory.

All three predict the same messy picture, and no experiment here separates them.

n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.title: Twenty billion parameters, and what would remain
n-what-was-shown-and-what-was-not--what-.intro: The level above gives the estimate and its two caveats. This one checks the arithmetic against what the paper actually ran, prices the data the same way, and separates the unknowns into two kinds: a curve nobody has measured, and costs the estimate does not cover at all.

chapters.title: What twenty billion assumes
chapters.body:
Both numbers in the estimate are assumptions, and it helps to see what they are assumptions against.

Width 10,000 stands in for one MLP layer of a large model. The layer this paper actually decomposed is 512 neurons wide, reading from a 128-dimensional residual stream [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. The hypothetical layer is around twenty times wider than anything tested here.

The [[expansion-factor]] of 100 does sit inside the range they ran. Most of the paper works with an 8× dictionary: 4,096 learned features for 512 neurons. The largest run goes to 131,072 features, an expansion of 256×.

Going wider than the layer is the whole point. The dictionary is deliberately overcomplete [[overcompleteness]], because the layer is assumed to carry more features than it has neurons [[superposition]].

So count the weights in the largest dictionary the paper trained. The encoder is $512 \times 131{,}072$, about 67 million numbers. The decoder is the same size, transposed. Roughly 134 million weights in total.

Twenty billion is about 150 times that.

Weights are only the resident cost. Adam carries two moment estimates per parameter, so the live training state is three copies of the tensor. The decoder's columns are held at unit L2 norm, so that the sparsity term of the objective cannot be cheapened by shrinking directions [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]] [[sparse-autoencoder-loss]]. That renormalization would run over a million columns of length 10,000, every step.

Neither matrix is sparse. The encoder is a dense linear map standing in for a sparse coding solver [[dictionary-learning]], and the sparsity lives in the activations rather than the weights [[sparse-autoencoder]]. The loop also periodically reinitializes units that have stopped firing, which means scoring loss over a large sample of inputs [[neuron-resampling]].

And this is one layer. The paper prices a single MLP and leaves the multiplication for the rest of a model unstated [[scaling-sparse-autoencoders]].

chapters.title: The data bill, in the paper's own numbers
chapters.body:
The data side has real numbers behind it here, and they scale badly in a different way.

To build the autoencoder's training set, the transformer is run over 40 million contexts from the Pile [[pile-dataset]]. Activation vectors are collected after the MLP's ReLU, 250 token positions are sampled from each context, and everything is shuffled so a batch draws from many documents [[autoencoder-training-dataset]].

That harvest is about 10 billion activation vectors. Training runs 1 million steps at batch size 8,192, which consumes just over 8 billion of them, sampled without replacement. The authors report that not repeating data mattered for results.

Set that beside the subject model, which saw 100 billion tokens. The reader consumed roughly a twelfth as many samples as the thing it reads — to decompose a 512-neuron layer.

The harvest also has to be held somewhere. Ten billion vectors of 512 numbers is on the order of 10 terabytes at two bytes a number. Keep the count fixed and widen the vectors to 10,000 dimensions, and the same corpus of activations is a couple of hundred terabytes.

Then the reason the count cannot be kept fixed. The paper defines a feature's density as the fraction of tokens on which it is nonzero [[feature-density]]. Plotted on a log axis, these densities are usually bimodal [[feature-density-histogram]]. The interpretable mode sits near one token in $10^5$ [[high-density-cluster]]. A left mode near $10^{-7}$ is almost entirely uninterpretable and is treated as an artifact of training rather than structure in the model [[ultralow-density-cluster]], distinct from units that simply never fire [[dead-neurons]].

Now count appearances. A feature firing on one token in a million turns up about 8,000 times in 8 billion samples. At $10^{-7}$ it turns up a few hundred times.

And widening the dictionary from 512 units to 131,072 kept surfacing rarer features, with no sign of the supply running out [[fig-67]].

chapters.title: What the optimism rests on
chapters.body:
The hope has two named supports. Both are thinner than the estimate they are meant to offset.

The first is outside work: an independent line of interim reports and a manuscript pursuing the same [[sparse-autoencoder]] approach [[cunningham-et-al-parallel-work]], prompted by the same earlier toy-model paper [[toy-models-of-superposition]]. The wording is careful. That work "seems to suggest" the approach "can work on somewhat larger models." How much larger is not said, and none of its numbers are reproduced here.

The second support is their own preliminary results, pointing the same way. No model is named. No figure is shown, and no metric is quoted. In a paper that otherwise puts its evidence on the page, this one is asserted and left there.

The consolation that follows is a claim of a different kind. If the agenda now turns on engineering and scale, the argument runs, that is what frontier labs are equipped for. This reassigns the difficulty to people likely to be good at it. It is not evidence that the method survives the trip.

There is also the question of how anyone would know. The authors say plainly that they have no systematic way to tell whether a run has extracted high-quality features [[recognizing-good-features]].

What they have instead is several imperfect signals read together [[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]. How much of the MLP's loss contribution the reconstruction recovers, measured against deleting the layer outright [[loss-recovered-by-features]] [[zero-ablation-baseline]]. Where a run lands on the tradeoff between sparsity and explained behavior [[sparsity-versus-explained-loss-sweep]]. How well two separately trained dictionaries' features match each other [[mean-max-cosine-similarity]].

One abstract alternative was tried and dropped, because it did not correlate with what they cared about [[information-based-metric]].

The contender they name for the job is having a language model write and score the explanations [[automated-interpretability]].

chapters.title: The curve nobody has fitted
chapters.body:
What would settle the feasibility question is a curve, and there is no curve [[scaling-laws-for-dictionary-learning]].

Two quantities need one. As the subject model grows, does the ideal [[expansion-factor]] stay constant, or drift? And how does the amount of data required move with model size? The paper wants scaling laws in the sense used for language model training: fitted relationships that let you read off what a larger run will need.

Fitting one requires something to put on the axis. That is a problem in itself.

The obvious target is the number of features in the layer. But widening the dictionary does not only find more features. It subdivides features already found into families covering the same territory more finely [[feature-splitting]]. The count does not settle down.

This is bound up with a picture that shifted during the work. The inherited model had features as discrete one-dimensional directions, pushed apart by interference into a roughly even spread [[isotropic-superposition-model]]. What the paper sees instead is features clumping into related groups, and possibly forming continuous higher-dimensional families [[feature-manifolds]] [[theories-of-superposition]]. Under some of those extensions, asking for the correct number of features may not be well posed [[correct-number-of-features]]. Under others there is a true number, and getting it wrong degrades gracefully into a coarser or finer view of the same things.

The algorithm whose curve you would be fitting is not settled either.

The refinements listed are specific [[algorithmic-improvements-for-sparse-autoencoders]]. Variational autoencoders. Sparsity-promoting priors and regularizers beyond a plain penalty on the hidden activations [[l1-sparsity-penalty]], including ones that encourage sparse interactions between features in different layers. Noise injection during training, which earlier work found raises neuron interpretability separately from any sparsity penalty [[noise-injection-for-interpretability]]. Harder schemes, such as keeping only the top $k$ activations, sit in the same neighborhood [[topk-activation]].

Change the objective and the curve you are measuring is a different curve.

chapters.title: Two costs outside the estimate
chapters.body:
Two costs sit outside the arithmetic entirely.

The first is attention. The reason this paper takes MLP activations as its target is that a one-layer attention-only transformer could be analyzed by rewriting it, without ever referring to its hidden states, whereas adding a ReLU MLP makes that impossible [[mlp-activations-as-target]]. Attention was not decomposed because, in that setting, it did not have to be.

That is not an argument that attention layers are free of the problem. The motivations for expecting superposition in an MLP — many more useful features than dimensions, most of them inactive on any given token [[feature-sparsity]] — apply to self-attention as well [[attentional-superposition]]. The paper says similar methods may extract useful structure there, then says a clear example has not been established, and points at its own earlier update posts. So this is a conjecture with attempts behind it and nothing to show.

If it holds, everything priced above covers half the model.

The second cost survives even complete success. Suppose sparse autoencoders fully solved superposition. The paper asks whether that finishes the job and answers no: turning microscopic, feature-level facts into a macroscopic understanding is a separate barrier [[scalability-of-analysis]].

This is the problem the paper opens with. The volume of internal state that has to be interpreted grows exponentially with model size, and cannot be searched or enumerated unless it breaks into components understandable on their own [[curse-of-dimensionality-in-interpretability]]. Decomposition is what makes the program tractable in principle [[mechanistic-interpretability]]. A million interpretable features in one layer is still a million things.

One route named is the same delegation to language models, which the authors say may not be fully satisfying, without spelling out why.

The other is coarser structure. Features fall into recurring kinds [[feature-motifs]], and into geometric clusters visible when the decoder directions are projected down [[umap-feature-map]]. Whether that adds up to a macroscopic account is not tested here.
